On the orders of the day:
Mr. JEAN-FRANCOIS POULIOT (Temis-couata): I regret that the Prime Minister and Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie King) is not in the house at the moment. I have received to-day the following telegram from Mr. Ludger Richard, the former mayor of Estcourt, Quebec. It refers to a matter which has been standing for several months, a boundary matter. The telegram reads:
What shall I do if my cattle and horses are seized? Pay? Let them be slaughtered? Or ask for permit? Notify by wire.
I wished to ask the Prime Minister what he would do if he were member for Temiscouata.
I shall have to ask the question of the Minister of Justice.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

speechtext:
My hon. friend sent a
copy of the telegram to the Department of External Affairs, or to some officer there, and they have supplied me with the following statement:
The United States has refunded the duty on certain cattle which were taken into the United States by Mr. Richard last year. The United States government have indicated that under their existing law duty must be paid on cattle taken into the United States regardless of whether or not the owner of the cattle is also the owner of land in the United States as well as in Canada. They have also indicated their readiness to permit the repeated entry of cattle on which duty has once been paid without charging further duty, in the case where a farmer owns one farm in Canada and an immediately adjoining and contiguous farm in the United States.
I understand the member for Temiscouata has been fully informed of the attitude of the United States government.

speechtext: I must ask for better order in all parts of the house. It is very difficult for me to hear, and for the minister to hear, as well as for the Hansard reporter. We are now on item 217.

I was amplifying the question asked by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar in regard to the purpose of the item. Will the minister at the same time explain the system of presenting the estimates to the house; to what extent each year we vote the amounts set forth, and to what extent we accept responsibility for future commitments?

May I add a word to that question?-because it covers the whole matter of the expenditures of this department. At the close of my brief remarks after the minister spoke I asked him to direct his attention to three questions: What have we received for the $90,000,000 voted in the past three years; has progress since 1936 been what it should, and has Canadian industry been used to the extent it should? So far as I can follow the statement made by the minister, parliament in the last three years has voted somewhere in the neighbourhood of $90,000,000 for defence, while the expenditure apparently has been in the neighbourhood of $60,000,000. In his statement the minister referred to this article and that article which had been ordered but not delivered. For the last two years the estimates have not included the words we were accustomed to see, "amount not required," very often because delivery had not taken place, so that the money could not be expended. I should be much obliged if in answering the questions already put to him the minister would make his remarks general on the subject of how the money is dealt with after being voted by parliament.

In regard to the question asked by the hon. member for Vancouver North, I think that point was dealt with fairly fully by the Minister of Finance on a previous occasion during the present session, when he explained why the $3,000,000 odd were required under the estimate now referred to in regard to capital expenditures.
I should like to place on record a brief statement with regard to the general principles followed as between capital and ordinary account.
The principle followed in selecting items which are shown in these estimates as charged to capital account was that all new structures, properties, ships, aircraft, armament and other equipment not considered replacements
[Mr. MacNeil.J
of like articles and which under normal conditions are expected to have an average life expectancy of at least ten years would be a charge to capital. In addition, service ammunition required for reserve purposes as against actual immediate purposes, as distinguished from that to be expended for practice purposes, was also considered a capital charge. Other equipment included under capital is that required to complete the complement of existing units or to provide for new units in the process of organization. Expenditures classified as ordinary are those for the replacement of existing equipment because of obsolescence or deterioration, ammunition for practice, expendable stores, salaries, pay and allowances, food supplies, transportation, printing, stationery, repairs to equipment and properties and other items of a strictly maintenance nature.
Then coming to the question of the hon. member for Yale, of course from the total of $90,000,000 voted during the last three years there must be deducted the annual maintenance cost of the Department of National Defence, as my hon. friend knows very well indeed. In regard to items ordered, in some cases it takes as long as three or four years to obtain equipment from available sources. My hon. friend himself ordered certain antiaircraft guns in 1935, before the previous administration left office, and they were delivered in 1938. In regard to certain other types of guns, mostly high calibre guns such as 6-inch or 9-2-inch, it took about four years to secure delivery, though I think now the situation is much improved.
In regard to commitments, for the first time in the estimates this year a definite statement is made in regard to the amount to which we are committed as against future years, the total being around $22,000,000 in the three services. That of course is subject every year to the will and decision of parliament. In other words, the sum in respect of these future commitments that would become an obligation next year of course would be included in whatever parliament decided should be the total vote for that year.
Whatever the government decide.

Yes,
subject to the will of parliament. It is a difficult situation; as a matter of fact I do not think any other department of government is up against the same difficulty in regard to obtaining equipment. We considered every possible way of doing it. Australia has established a trust fund in London for similar purposes, but my information is that we could not follow a similar

Supply-National Defence
practice because of our audit act. This seems to be the only possible way of obtaining the necessities of national defence; that is, frankly to inform parliament. As I say, what is provided in that regard is subject of course to the decision and will of all future parliaments as to what we shall be committed to in future years-not necessarily next year. Some of the commitments I mentioned were incorporated in the estimates of 1938-39, and were not so definitely and clearly expressed in the estimates of last year as they are now. Hon. members will find in all the estimates this year the amount of commitments specifically set out. We shall therefore know exactly what the commitment will be for three or four years ahead in regard to the estimates of last year, plus the estimates of this year.
These are the estimates for 1939-40 are they not?
Yes.

The explanation the minister has given clarifies the situation so far as 1939-40 is concerned. Under the estimates of
1937-38 certain munitions were ordered, and presumably moneys were set aside and voted by parliament for that purpose. When delivery was not made, what happened to that money?-because presumably it was not expended. Why did it not appear in the estimates of the following year as an amount not expended?

This item provides for annual sinking fund to retire, with interest, moneys borrowed for capital expenditures. Would the minister give a sample list, if I may so describe it, of articles which would be included in capital expenditures?

I do not think I could do that exactly. It was worked out when the estimates were adopted in the first place by the technical advisers of the department. But generally speaking capital sums are expended on durable supplies and equipment.

But what would they
include?
I believe I mentioned that in my statement.
The list would not have to be complete. I should be content with an example.

Well,
fortifications would be one example. Then, certain kinds of weapons have a life of twenty years or more. Certain ships would be included-possibly destroyers-with a life of, say, twenty years. In fact the term would include anything not to be expended in the ordinary process of carrying on from year to year.

I understand that. But
let us consider a gun, or some type of artillery which in peace time would have a life of five years. Would the department limit the amortization of that item to five years, or would it take the general figure of twenty years or ten years, and make out a general amortization in that way? If it is not done in that way, how is it done?

The
general amortization period is ten years, but it is quite possible that some of the more durable articles would extend over twenty-five, thirty, forty or, in the case of fortifications, possibly to a hundred years.

With further reference to
the question asked by the leader of the opposition in regard to duties paid-

And that includes sales
tax.

Yes, this amount of something over $3,000,000 represents the amount the department pays. But the different units throughout Canada are continually purchasing supplies from England and other countries.
[Mr Manion.]
and they, too, are paying large sums in duties. I think the chief objection has been to the duties paid by individual units. Has any representation been made to the customs branch in an attempt to have either the duties cancelled or considerably reduced? These charges are a great burden on the militia units throughout the country. I believe the excuse offered is that the goods can be purchased in Canada. Theoretically that may be true, but practically I believe it is not true. In order to get the necessary equipment, that which they consider best, the units have to go outside of Canada. I suggest that a careful survey be made by the militia branch in an effort to have these duties lowered or cancelled so far as they apply to militia units struggling along on a very small amount of money.

If the hon. member for Royal could see the correspondence I have he would be immediately assured that the Department of National Defence is taking every possible step to carry out his suggestion. The only possible remedy we have at the present moment is by way of rebate, and in the last two years this has been granted in several cases. In regard to the general question of uniforms, there are two points of view. There is the point of view put forward by the hon. member, with which I sympathize, and there is the point of view of the Canadian citizen who produces uniforms in Canada. He would naturally object to the abolition of the duty on uniforms imported from the mother country, for example. I can assure my hon. friend this matter has been actively before the government, but so far the representations which he is advancing have not been successful.

Is it necessary to impose the
sales tax?

That is
a matter of general government policy which I cannot discuss at this time.
My hon. friend is speaking to the converted. Was there an application for rebate in that case?
No.
I think it would have been successful.

This thing has happened not once but several times in Hamilton. In some cases rebates were applied for but were refused. I brought the matter up last year in the debate on the speech from the throne, and on the defence estimates earlier this session, and I bring it up again to-day. It seems to me it is something that could be arranged. A penalty should not be placed on the head of a man who wants to be a good citizen.
I quite agree with my hon. friend. Will he be good enough to let me have the details of that particular case?

I should like to supplement the remarks of the hon. member for Hamilton West and the hon. member for Royal. The government should give serious consideration to these cases. As the minister knows, many of these militia officers are making monetary sacrifices, as well as giving considerable time and hard work to building up their units. They should receive consideration from the government, and certainly they should not have to pay duty on goods which are not produced in Canada. No sales tax should be charged on goods they buy in Canada for their own units out of their own pockets.

I desire to support what has been said in connection with securing rebates or the cancellation of the duty. As an example, I should like to cite what occurred in my own town. It was decided to form a Highland band. There is no regiment there, but by public subscription and through contributions made by friends of the same race and others kindly disposed, sufficient money was collected to clothe the band. Uniforms
were ordered as well as band equipment, and when they arrived there was a heavy bill of duty to be paid. A rebate was applied for, but unfortunately it was not granted. It seems to me that in cases of this kind there should be a uniform ruling that rebates will be allowed or that the duty will be taken off. As the minister already knows, there is a strong body of public opinion in favour of action of this kind. The loss of revenue would be quite small, the expense to those immediately interested being out of all proportion to the revenue derived. I know the minister is interested in this matter and I hope he will be able to follow it up with some success and obtain either a rebate in each case or cancellation of the duty.

While I sympathize to a certain extent with the views expressed by the leader of the opposition and other members on the other side of the house, nevertheless I do know that considerable military equipment is made in Canada, especially woollen military cloth, which is made in Brantford. Very good tartans are now being made in Brantford and other parts of Canada, and being a Scotsman I do not like to have to pay a duty on kilts.
What about sporrans?

These
goods are being made in Canada, and Canadian industry should receive every consideration. I must take a view entirely opposite to that expressed by hon. members of the opposition. I am not a free trader with respect to these or any other goods, and I am surprised to hear that so many members of the opposition have suddenly become free traders.
With respect to Scotch goods.

It is contrary to their general views. I am satisfied it is not the best thing for Canada. Those of us who love our country and who are prepared to join military units should be ready to encourage and protect Canadian industry, and, if necessary, pay a small duty.

There is a certain inconsistency about the views expressed by my hon. friend. I certainly agree that supplies should be bought in Canada where that is possible. But certain of these supplies, particularly those referred to by hon. members on this side, cannot be obtained in Canada. I am thinking particularly of certain things required by an officer of the king when he is promoted, such as badges, marks of rank and other items which require gold bullion. So far as my information goes, these are not
Supply-National Defence

obtainable in Canada, at least not of the quality desired. When, an officer receives a promotion and these necessities are brought into Canada, it seems to me to be unreasonable that he should have to pay duty on them.
There is one difficulty. Fpr instance, take blue serge for naval uniforms. If this material were exempt from duty, the exemption might cover a tremendous territory.
We make serge.
We are sympathetic toward this matter, but the difficulties are real.
I am referring particularly to gold trouser stripes, epaulettes and insignia of various kinds.

I believe this is one of the most entertaining interludes we have had during the present session. The argument which has been advanced by the Conservative opposition applies to many other things in which many of us are interested. I agree with the plea which has been made, but if we are to adopt this principle it should be extended to a much wider field.

As a matter of fact there is nothing new about this proposal, because rebates of all kinds are allowed. I may tell the hon. member for Rosetown-dliggar that in the past rebates have been allowed on hospital goods and various other articles. We all want to build up Canadian industry; in that regard we all agree with the hon. member for Brantford, but at the same time this is not a commercial proposition any more than a hospital is. Many exceptions have been made, even by those who believe in protecting our industries, from the point of view, it may be, of charity, in this case loyalty, without in any way infringing upon our fundamental view as to what it is best to do for our industries.
The unfair thing about it is, that officers giving their services voluntarily are taxed by the country for so doing.
Do I understand that this item will appear now from year to year, either this amount or probably an increased amount for the next ten years?

Yes, a similar amount for the next nine years unless the expenditure chargeable to capital account be increased. Then, of course, the interest and sinking fund charges on the capital would be

increased, in accordance with the decision made by the government and parliament from year to year.

Does that mean that in voting these estimates in their present form we are undertaking commitments in respect of a program extending over ten years, with very little opportunity to review it in discussion when the departmental estimates are under consideration?

No. We are only committing ourselves to the $3,000,000 odd and the $29,000,000 of capital expenditure in this year's estimates. But in addition to that, there is set out in the estimates a total commitment for future years of $22,000,000 for the three services; we are committing ourselves to that amount, subject to the decision of future parliaments. It is to be expended over three or four years after 1939^40.

In reality, to use a colloquialism, we are buying on time something for which we ordinarily would pay cash. We are spreading the payments for capital expenditure over a period of years instead of paying' it all in one year. Is that right?

Capital expenditure for the year. My hon. friend is confusing two things. The capital expenditures are part of our $60,000,000 for this year, but instead of paying in one sum we are spreading it over ten years, and we are absorbing the sinking fund charges in the amount of $3,000,000 odd per year. Apart from that, we are committing the people of Canada to this expenditure of $22,000,000, which is set out clearly in the estimates. That is entirely apart from ordinary or capital expenditure, and must be taken care of year by year by whoever is in authority.

Apparently we are dealing with a long-range program. I appreciate the minister's difficulty in planning any such program, and I do not object to it, but, with reference to the approval of parliament of a long-range program would it not be appropriate for the minister now to disclose what he has in mind? There could then be a general discussion of the fundamental principles of a long-range program, particularly with regard to its strategical objectives.

I think I can tell my hon. friend what representations have been made to the minister, 'but first I want to make it clear that this is not a question of government policy; it does not commit any government. These are representations made with regard to a long-range defence policy for the Dominion of Canada.

Supply-National Defence
The advice given by the technical advisers is that a peace-time establishment of certain proportions would be required in Canada. The progress that has been made during the last three years has been within the framework of the estimated requirements, a detailed list of which has been given to the house already. I think it is fitting, in reply to my hon. friend's question, that I should state what the officers of the department recommend. Whether that would be the ultimate policy would possibly be a matter for a committee such as my hon. friend and the leader of the opposition suggested the other day, where it could be discussed in great detail by representatives of all parties in both houses.
The ultimate objective which the navy has set out for Canada is to build up a naval force of eighteen destroyers, nine on each coast; eight anti-submarine vessels, four on each coast; sixteen minesweepers, eight on each coast; eight motor torpedo vessels, to be used on the east coast only; two parent vessels, one for the destroyers on the west coast and one for the motor torpedo boats on the east coast.
Covering a period of how many years?

There is no objective in point of time. It depends on our resources and financial limitations. I am only giving the advice which the technical officers offered to the minister or the government, what in their view we should have. It is a matter that could be considered carefully by a committee which the leader of the opposition suggested the other day. Then with regard to base defences, to maintain this naval force there would be required two naval bases, one at Halifax and one at Esquimalt, and two subsidiary bases, one at Sydney and one at Prince Rupert, to maintain the naval units mentioned. A personnel for the program suggested by the naval authorities would be required, consisting of 6,000 officers and ratings. The existing strength is 1,965 officers and ratings.
The capital expenditure which would be involved to achieve the objectives which they have recommended is $68,860,000, and the maintenance cost, once we had reached that objective, would be $13,500,000 a year.

Including both interest
and depreciation?
Yes, as I have just explained.
Would that be the complete naval vote?
Yes.

Would that cover all naval services?

annual maintenance cost of all naval services. It would not cover the replacement cost of ships that had to be bought. It would be the annual maintenance cost.

That would be our total
naval vote each year?
Mr.	MACKENZIE	(Vancouver):	Yes,
and this year it is $8,500,000.

Mr.	MACKENZIE	(Vancouver):	Yes,
definitely. Suppose we had to replace a destroyer or an anti-submarine vessel, the capital expenditure would be increased. The annual cost of maintaining the units set out as the objective would be $13,500,000.

No, this
is the advice given by the naval chief of staff perhaps after consultation with the honorary advisory committee. But the advisory committee as such is not responsible for these recommendations. The recommendations come from the three permanent chiefs of staff.

If the plan of amortization outlined in this item were adopted and the $68,000,000 of naval capital expenditure were amortized in this same way, amounting to over $7,000,000 a year, it would increase the naval vote, including capital equipment, to something like $21,000,000.

If the
financing were done in the same way; but there might be alternative ways, loans or some other way.
It would be an increased amount. I have not worked it out that way, but it certainly would be an increased amount.
Before the minister leaves the naval plan, may I ask if this list of ships which he has just announced is the list which the technical officers say is required at once?
This is the list of ships which our naval advisers inform us are absolutely necessary for the proper and adequate defence of Canada.
At the present time?
Well, of course, if we could get them at the present time-
No, but do they say that these ships are needed adequately to defend Canada at the present time?

This is given us as the peace time establishment; there is no question about that. At this stage I might set out the objectives in regard to the militia as they have been presented to us. In the first place, to complete the approved plans for coastal defence: The plans for defence of both coasts were drawn up by our own staff officers in conjunction with the best expert we could obtain from the war office in England, and after very careful consultation, so that there is nothing haphazard or fortuitous; every single calibre of gun and every site has been decided on with the very best advice obtainable. Next, to provide for the antiaircraft defence of centres estimated to be exposed to air attack.
My hon. friend started by saying "in regard to the militia." Does this refer to the militia?

Yes. I am now dealing with the militia. That defence will be through coastal batteries. Also, to provide the principal items of armament and equipment for the several fortress garrisons, a force of two divisions and ancillary troops for the defence of Canada in Canada. There has been some criticism of the armament for mobile divisions. I want to emphasize the fact that the whole purpose of these divisions

as planned in 1935-36 is to be mobile within Canada, to supplement fortress garrisons, to aid in the defence of Canada if necessary.
The active militia is organized at the present time as follows: permanent force and one cavalry division and six divisions with ancillary troops and fortress garrisons. Peace establishment of the permanent force, 6,928; non-permanent force, 86,000. Present strength of the permanent force, 4,211; non-permanent active militia, 51,659. An increase of about 2,800 would be required in the permanent force to carry out the recommendations which have been made. No net increase of the non-permanent active militia is contemplated in these recommendations, although there might be an increase necessary for fortress garrisons on the coasts.

They are not being manufactured in government-owned arsenals-
Quite a lot of them are.

The experience of the great war shows that state organization and coordination of production is essential for the rapid mobilization of manufacturing capacity and the maintenance of supplies on an adequate scale. I think the minister should tell us how he is going to have these field guns made in Canada, and I think he should tell us about the anti-aircraft guns. Apparently we cannot get them in England or the United States, and we are doing nothing about manufacturing them here. The house and the country should know what the government proposes to do about anti-aircraft guns.

In regard to the first question asked by my hon. friend, I can only tell him that as yet no decision has been arrived at. In regard to anti-aircraft guns, every possible source of supply has been and is being explored.

That does not get us anywhere at all. The minister says no decision has been arrived at, yet a few moments ago

he said he hoped to be able to manufacture at least one kind of artillery in Canada this year.

We should know what that plan is, and it does not help us a bit in connection with the anti-aircraft guns to say every source has been explored. That does not set up guns to defend Ottawa or Quebec or Vancouver; it is just evading the question. The minister said the same thing earlier in the session with regard to rifles; he said the government had not yet decided what was to be done about rifles. Yet we have militia officers openly saying that many of their rifles are not a bit of use; that they are war-time rifles that are not accurate. Still that is what our defence forces are equipped with. We should know what the government propose to do about getting proper equipment with which these men can fight. If men do not have proper equipment they cannot fight properly, as the minister knows from his own experience. Each of us who served in France saw the same thing happen. My battalion went to France with Oliver equipment and Ross rifles, and they had to go and scrounge Webb equipment and Enfield rifles, from other units, or from salvaging dumps, or in other ways. It simply means young Canadians are going to be slaughtered, if trouble comes, because they are not properly equipped. This house should know how the government propose to meet this lack of equipment.
In regard to rifles I want to correct the erroneous and improper statement made by the hon. member. To-day in Canada we are equipped with rifles.

Before we leave this suggested $30,000,000 arsenal I should like to address a question or two to the minister, because we are bound to hear more of this idea. In connection with this plan was it estimated how long it would take such an arsenal in peace time completely to fill the needs in connection with Canadian defence? Before the minister anwers this question, and in conjunction with it, did the plan anticipate what would be done with that arsenal when

the defence needs of Canada had been provided for, or did they envisage a war before that time? Because if we had such a plant and went into production, as we assuredly would in a time like this, to build up as quickly as possible the maximum amount of armament needed for the defence of Canada, I am wondering about the commitments in which we might become involved. I say that because somebody would promptly make it his business to find work for that arsenal. Would the government of Canada go into the production of armaments for export, or would they divert that arsenal into competition with other heavy industries? I should like to know what has been visualized.

The plan did not visualize anything definite with respect to the time factor. It would have been impossible to do so, because certain calibres of material would take a long time to get into production. As a matter of fact the experience of Australia, to which reference has been made, has been disappointing. My hon. friend must know, and all hon. members know, that in 1935 or 1936, public opinion would not have supported, nor would hon. members, the expenditure of $30,000,000 or more for a government arsenal in Canada. I am not so sure that they would support it to-day. But the point is that even if we had received support in parliament in 1935 or 1936 for the expenditure of $30,000,000 for a government arsenal, we could not be in production at this moment on some of our primary requirements for national defence. It is a tremendously difficult problem. There are two considerations, first of which is the will of parliament, the financial resources of the nation; and the second is our ability to produce these things. I have no doubt Canadian industry is as well qualified as any other industry in the world to provide our essential requirements. The general opinion in Canada seems to be, in the first place, so far as possible to develop government arsenals, and, in the second place, to cooperate with private industry.
I wish to have it understood that I was not suggesting the scheme should have been proceeded with. I was trying to find out the difficulties involved.

It is difficult for me to sit and listen to this discussion and not say something. I am sure all hon. members from British Columbia must realize there are many industrial shops which are either not working at all or are on half or part time. I wonder if it would be an impertinence to suggest to the minister that the managements of these shops throughout Canadanot only those in British Columbia-be tentatively asked how long it would take them to put them in order to produce small arms of various kinds. I make this merely as a suggestion.
We know that no government or minister can proceed in a course which is contrary to public opinion. In response to, public opinion a few years ago the air force of Canada was practically scrapped. That was a tragedy, and we realize it to-day. Our country is vulnerable to air attack at the west and north; we have no air service on the western and northern coasts which could save us. We in the north have never thought that at any time we could be in danger. But with fifteen to twenty planes over our heads daily in the towns of Dawson, White Horse and Mayo, we realize that there would be no difficulty at all in the planes of other nations establishing an air base in our part of the country. None of us wants war, the women probably less than any other group in the country. But at the same time we must prepare. In a time when nations of the world are led by madmen, what are we going to do if we do not support the government in its defence program? At the same time of course we should demand that the government, whatever party may be in power, do the best it possibly can, and that it be honest with itself-because if it is honest with itself it will be honest with the nation and with the people who comprise the nation. So far as I am concerned, in every way, shape and form, privately or publicly, by my actions or my voice-and in this I am supported by the people in my community-I would support the minister and the government in making every preparation and in doing all they possibly can to defend this country when the time comes-as I am very much afraid it is going to come to all of us.

Notwithstanding the remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver South, I am still of the opinion that it would be a grave mistake for this government to enter upon the building of a large arsenal. It is true that in Great Britain there are a number of government arsenals, but they are merely pilot plants and are also used for purposes of research. To-day the great bulk of armaments in Great Britain are being built by private industry. As the minister has pointed out, they are decentralizing the manufacture of armaments and scattering their manufacturing establishments throughout the country. The minister and other hon. members have said that one large plant is particularly vulnerable to attack. That is a good reason why there should not be one large

arsenal instead of a number of smaller ones. Besides, why build an arsenal and ask working men to give up their homes and establish homes in a new district, when some day the manufacture of armaments will not be required? Why would it not be better to build armaments in Canadian plants which are now closed, plants which have employed the best mechanics in the world and which are adjacent to the homes of the workmen? It would be far better to have armaments manufactured in plants of that kind than to break up the homes of working men and require them to establish homes in other places.
It has been suggested that armaments should be produced as soon as possible. I think all hon. members will agree that to convert privately-owned plants into plants capable of manufacturing armaments would take only half the time required to build new ones. I still believe we should be loath to proceed with any large-scale building of an arsenal.

I did not intend to leave the impression that we should manufacture all our munitions in government arsenals in a time of war. But to-day, although the department has made a survey of about a thousand plants-I do not exactly know how many-
I believe the figure is 1597.

-not one of those plants knows how to make these guns. If we had had an arsenal built to act as a pilot plant, and capable of manufacturing small quantities, even at a fairly high cost, we should be in a position to-day to give instructions to others as to what they would have to do. They would have the necessary tools and equipment. If we go into the manufacture of armaments to-day, where are we going to get the tools?
May I place on record a paragraph appearing at page 296 of the Canadian Defence Quarterly, 1936-37:
In time of war the government factories would be quite inadequate, but in peace time they serve as places where a technical staff can be trained, and in the course of that training it is arranged that the ordinary peace-time requirements of munitions by the fighting services are produced. The factories are also organized as the centres from which manufacturing details would be circulated to the commercial industries should necessity require their conversion from their normal pursuits.
That outlines the principle underlying the use of arsenals. We find ourselves without arsenals, and we must have arms. That is all there is to it. We are going to have to be armed for probably twenty years, and we should get busy and get these arsenals going

so that we may be able to keep up with the changes that are taking place from time to time. In the meantime we ought to take this $60,000,000 on order, and get the manufacturers of this country busy on making these things so that we shall not always be undefended as we are at the present time.

I agree absolutely with the hon. member for Brantford City. There are many plants in this country which are either equipped or could be equipped in a short time to manufacture different types of arms and equipment. I could cite one plant, Messrs. John Bertram and Sons of Dundas. This plant is one hundred per cent Canadian, and it is affiliated with a large plant in the United States which is manufacturing large guns for the United States navy, and I believe also for the army. In a short time it could be ready to manufacture the 25-pounder or any size of gun the department might require.

There are several points in this discussion which should be cleared up. I do not think anyone is suggesting that we should develop arsenals in Canada capable of making all calibres of guns, but there is good ground for the argument that the manufacture of small arms and ammunition should be under state control. A committee known as the Skelton committee was appointed, and one of the paragraphs of its report deals with the idea of a complete state monopoly with regard to armament manufacture. The exact wording of the report is:
Whether, putting aside the idea of a complete state monopoly, there might be a case for some moderate extension of present government arsenals-in order to produce, for example, a certain limited selection of articles, for which the government would be the only purchaser and might need a continuous supply, and for which no private manufacturing equipment now exists in Canada-is a matter which the government might wish to consider as a matter of policy.
I should like to know to Vhat extent the government intends to carry out the recommendation contained in the report of the Skelton committee. The members of that committee gave the matter conscientious study. This committee was made up of men in the service for whom we all have the highest regard.
Objection has been made to the concentration of manufacturing facilities. We have learned from our inquiry into these matters that the big job in making small arms is tooling the plant. If the government is to place an order with private industry for small arms, the government must stand almost completely the expense of tools, jigs and gauges. I shall not go over the arguments which have

Could not the equipment be moved with ease to another plant?

Production plans would be seriously interfered with. As I understand it, the production layout is a very intricate matter, and it would be extraordinarily difficult to move them. I imagine that rather than do that the government would undertake measures of defence for the plant. They would ring it about with anti-aircraft guns as is done in the United States.
The defence council, made up of outstanding experts on defence in Canada, also took the position that it would be in the interests of this dominion to have a limited development of arsenals for supply. This would prove a yardstick, as it were, for the cooperation with private enterprise and would ensure to the dominion a continuous source of supply. There would also be a guarantee of absolute control over all sources of supply.
While there might be objection to state monopoly in connection with the manufacture of all armaments, there are decided objections to having a private monopoly in this connection. We have had experience in this regard in Canada. There was a private monopoly in connection with the manufacture of the Ross rifle at the outbreak of the last war. Before the dominion government extricated itself from its contractual obligations with the Ross Rifle Company and Sir Charles Ross personally, it cost the government some millions of dollars. Before we are committed to any 71492-260i
long-range program, I think the minister should outline this matter very carefully at this time. I do not want to enter into an argument with regard to the Bren gun, but these points have been canvassed by the defence council and the Skelton committee. They advocate state control over the manufacture of small arms and ammunition, at the same time retaining the cooperation of private enterprise.
With regard to the point raised by the hon. member for Yukon, I realize that aircraft must be made by private industry. No government could undertake the manufacture of aircraft. I realize also that certain calibres of guns would have to be secured from other sources of supply. But the government could manufacture pistols, rifles, light machine guns, and even the heavy machine guns which are now obtained in Great Britain. Any industry would require aid from the government in connection with tooling, and unquestionably this business would be placed on a cost-plus basis. In the light of our experience I think it is true that government arsenals could be opened up for certain lines of manufacture at no greater cost than would be involved in placing orders with private industry. But the cooperation of private industry would have to be retained. For example, the manufacture of shells does not require a long pre-production period, such as is required for the manufacture of small arms.

Production in our arsenals has been increased six-fold in connection with certain articles and fourfold in connection with others. A gauge plant has been built in the province of Quebec, and at the present time we intend to go ahead with the development of the Lindsay arsenal. As far as my personal feelings are concerned, I should like to see all our small arms and ammunition manufactured in government arsenals, but there are other definite types of material of which we do not require a sufficient quantity to justify economical production by the government.

While the time may have come for the establishment of government arsenals-I do not know that it has, but I am ready to take the opinion of those who should know-I do believe that apart from their purpose as pilot plants to guide private industry, sufficient arsenals could not be put on a productive basis in time of emergency for a sum short of $100,000,000. War is always an emergency. Private industry is now equipped to manufacture munitions of all kinds if the proper guidance is given. I agree heartily with the hon. member for Brantford City and the hon. member for Wentworth.

If without much criticism or discussion we give approval to the recommendations presented this morning, we shall be committing ourselves to an annual expenditure of over seventy million dollars to meet both the capital and ordinary expenditures of the department. Am I right in that?
Suppose we floated a loan for $175,000,000; the cost of that loan would be entirely apart from the annual maintenance cost of the three services, which I mentioned as being $53,500,000.

If that is so, and we are contemplating these very large expenditures over a period of years, the argument advanced for manufacturing as much of the small arms as possible in government arsenals, even if it requires some capital outlay to complete and equip them, is a very sound argument, because we are actually considering a long-term defence program. We have been discussing the defence estimates this morning on a basis entirely different from that of former years. We are actually considering on the suggestion of the minister, and I think his suggestion is
XMr. Marsh.]
a good one, that we should lay out a longterm program. If we are laying out a longterm plan we should consider ways and means of producing at least small arms and other equipment which is easily manufactured in our own arsenals; because, after all, undoubtedly there is a widespread feeling that profits should be taken out of war and out of preparedness for war. Certainly we should not pass over these estimates, as perhaps we are inclined to do, without giving further thought to ways and means and, if necessary, to expenditures required, to enable this country to get away as rapidly as possible from the private manufacture of arms. I am sure that would meet with the desires generally of the Canadian people. If, therefore, we are to enter upon a defence program extending over a period of time we should consider ways and means of taking the profits both out of war and out of preparedness for war, and doing as much of this work as we possibly can in our own arsenals. That is the policy which is being gradually introduced in European countries, where of course they are spending much more than we are on armaments.

Are the dominion arsenals
to be expanded so that they can manufacture any type of equipment? We have certain Canadian National railway shops which could be used for the manufacture of at least some of our requirements. Is any attempt being made to use these shops?

Replying to the first question, it would take a tremendous capital sum to equip the arsenals for all types of manufacture. I think it is proper to develop the dominion arsenals for the manufacture of ammunition and small arms if a fairly permanent production is required. As to other supplies of which our requirements would be limited, it would be difficult to justify from an economic point of view the large capital expenditures involved in any grand arsenal scheme for that purpose. As to my hon. friend's second question, the department has for the last several months been in consultation with both railway companies with reference to the point he raised.

The government does a lot of consulting on these things, but has any action been taken to use the Canadian National shops for the manufacture of military equipment?

Not up
to date.

We have really drifted off
into an argument as to whether we should have state or private manufacture of munitions in Canada. But the real point is this: According to the minister's own statement, we need a great deal of equipment, and we cannot get it. We cannot buy it in England; I do not know whether we can buy it in the United States, but certainly we cannot produce it here. Mobile army requirements are listed as 500 field guns, 340 antitank equipments, 544 infantry mortars, 60 medium howitzer equipments, 20 medium gun equipments. What is the government going to do about supplying this equipment? Am I right when I say that we have not the equipment in Canada to equip fully one brigade with modern armament? Is that wrong? If we cannot equip in Canada one brigade, what is the use of talking about a division here or a division there, or a brigade here or a brigade there? What does the minister propose to do about getting this equipment which he says he cannot get at the present time?
The prospects for obtaining supplies are much better now than they were a year ago.
From Great Britain?
Yes.

With
regard to the argument that the manufacture of armaments should be given to workmen of the idle shops of the Canadian National Railways, I can see no reason whatsoever why those workingmen should receive any more consideration than the workingmen of closed factories in Brantford and many other cities of this dominion.

They have not the
machinery and are not equipped for that kind of work.

There are many plants in Canada, I am sure, which have equipment just as good as the equipment in the shops of the Canadian National Railways. If any orders for armaments are being given, the closed factories in the city of Brantford should receive just as much consideration as the idle shops of the Canadian National Railways.

There is no need to restrict the opposition to that idea to hon. members from Toronto. In Winnipeg we have two
large Canadian National shops, well equipped, and with a personnel experienced in this type of manufacturing during the last war. The men there have not been employed on full time for a matter of years. These shops-* and I speak only of the Canadian National Railways-are the responsibility of the Canadian government and the Canadian people. It has been contended that in time of war transportation will be speeded up to such an extent that these shops will be needed for their regular business at full capacity, and that argument has been put forward in opposition to the use of the shops for other than railway purposes. It is urged that if in peace time we establish in these railway shops a base of armament supplies, then when the need for armaments is greatest we should have to take these men away from the manufacture of armaments and put them back on the maintenance of rolling stock. Certainly the railroad is a peace-time organization, although there are arguments in favour of the use of the government-owned shops.

There are needed 544 infantry mortars: can we make those in Canada? There are needed 16 medium howitzers, 20 medium gun equipments, 500 field guns, 348 anti-tank equipments:	can we
make those in Canada? If so, why do we not make them here? There is much unemployment in this country; surely we can put our men to work instead of ordering the equipment from some other country. I notice that there is on file in the department a memorandum to the effect that the approximate cost of a factory to manufacture 25-pounders would be $2,000,000; that estimate includes carriage works and other necessary accessories to turn out the complete weapons and wheels ready for use. It states that approximately eight months would elapse before delivery of guns begins, and if the plants were employed on production of 25-pounder guns they could be delivered at the rate of about two a week. If we can make these guns and equipment, let us do so.

I may be wrong, but it
strikes me that the very nature of this subject is such as to make open discussion inadvisable, with the press and other agencies capable of distributing detailed knowledge which should be left to relatively private sources. I do not suggest that there are not some things which could be discussed here openly, in a general way, but if it is a question of equipping ourselves adequately, why should

we, through open discussion in this house, expose to others a full knowledge of that equipment?

I wish to say a word or
two with regard to the railway shops. I have had several communications from men in the shops, as well as from organizations representing the men, stating that, particularly in the Canadian National shops in the Winnipeg district, there can be produced certain armaments which are desired at the present time by the government. I do not know much about the mechanical features of the production of armaments, but one assumes, when he receives letters and communications from men engaged in the machine shops and the organizations representing them, they know what they are talking about. During the last war, between 1915 and 1918, railway shops in the Winnipeg area were producing shells-
Shell casings.

-and a large amount of other equipment. If the government is in a position to equip and willing to equip private plants with tools to produce armaments, is there any reason why shops already partly equipped for the purpose could not be further equipped so as to give the employees a little more work than they are now getting? I have no objection to further provision so far as Brantford is concerned; these men, even in the city of Brantford, are deserving of every consideration. But when we have shops owned and operated by the government, as are the Canadian National shops, and partly equipped for this purpose, I believe that our first duty is to the employees in those shops.
No, no.

Oh, yes. As a matter of fact our government has been extremely kind to the private manufacturer so far as railway equipment orders are concerned. In a return brought down to this house a few weeks ago it was shown that about ten times as much equipment for the Canadian National Railways was made in private shops as was made in the government shops, although the latter could have manufactured a large part of it. We have these railway shops, partly equipped, which could with perhaps slight adjustments produce work which the government wants done and give employment to the men. If there are factories or other shops which are also in a position to produce equipment, I have no objection to contracts being given

to them as well. Has any progress been made as between the minister and, say, both railway companies in the matter of utilizing the railway shops for the production of armaments?

All I
can tell my hon. friend is that the managements of both railways have been consulted with reference to what they can do. There is no doubt that they can do what my hon. friend says they can do; the question is as to the distribution of our requirements as between these shops, private industry, and government arsenals. It is purely a matter of policy. Objection has been raised in some quarters, among railway officials themselves, to utilizing their shops for production such as this, on the assumption that it might interfere with their normal activities in case of emergency. Whether or not that view is well-founded is a matter on which I would not care to venture a personal opinion.

Is it the intention of the government to use every effort to work in cooperation with the railway companies and to give, if necessary to both companies, and particularly to the Canadian National Railways, an opportunity of producing in their shops whatever in the way of armaments they are capable of producing?

That
opportunity has already been offered by way of conference and consultation with those who are responsible for the direction of policy of the railways. Although nothing definite has resulted up to the present, I shall be very glad to continue towards some degree of cooperation.
I understand from the minister that evidently, as between the railway shops, the parties have not been able to come together on a working basis?

On a
definite policy.
Well, is it not possible that the government might come to some arrangement?

We did not have any concrete problem which we could submit to them-anything definite so far that we could ask them to do.

When the committee rose we were discussing the question of policy involved in this item, particularly in view of the fact that the department evidently contemplates planning for a long-range program. I think there was substantial agreement among the members of the committee that the staff should have opportunity to engage in a long-range program. But even at this stage of this session it is still desirable that a a special committee of the house, whether informal or on whatever basis it may be organized, should have the opportunity of discussing in detail questions of policy. In the light of the discussion this morning, the point made by the hon. member for Essex East, that perhaps we are venturing too far afield in this discussion, was not, in my view, well taken; for none of us has shown any disposition to go beyond the limits of or the information contained in the departmental report. Certain questions are matters of public policy. Sources of supply are certainly matters of public policy, even if there be no desire to question the minister or his officers in regard to specifications or details of construction, disposition of units or supplies, or anything that might be regarded as a military or naval secret. But we are discussing a matter of policy in regard to the manufacture of armaments. Under private manufacture as we have now established it in Canada-and we have now a virtual monopoly of small arms manufacture in Canada on the part of private enterprise-no provision is made for the training of mechanics. In time of emergency we shall be sorely pressed in Canada for men trained in the factory operations necessary for the support of men in the field. I repeat that it takes about eight men in the factory to maintain one machine gun in the field, forty men for a
combat tank in the field and about sixty men for a pursuit plane. These statistics are based upon computations made by the German general staff. Private enterprise is necessarily limited in its activities to profit-making operations; they have to have a profit in order to continue operations. They have to keep profit-making considerations in view. They cannot undertake responsibility with regard to training of apprentices. I do not see where Canada can possibly obtain the trained mechanics necessary to the provision of a constant supply of aircraft, munitions, or weapons of certain calibre.
Put in older men. There are enough older men who cannot get a job at the present time.
I have been in touch with an aircraft manufacturer in Canada, known quite well to my hon. friend; he knows that that manufacturer has had extreme difficulty in getting trained men-
Because he wanted young men.
It became necessary for him to apply to the immigration department to bring in from the United States men with special training in certain machine shop operations.
Yes, three or four key men.

Yes, the number was
small. On the other hand that same manufacturer, for whom I have great respect, had to take a great deal of trouble to train young men. I have no reason to question his statement that actually in the first contract- perhaps the minister will corroborate this- he had to face the expectation of a loss because of his desire to train young Canadians in that highly specialized field of endeavour, rather than to import specialists. In view of that experience I suggest that we should expand our dominion arsenals along certain lines rather than rely entirely on private enterprise, and that the department should assume some responsibility, even by employing rotation, so that young men seeking this technical training may be introduced to the machine shop practice peculiar to the manufacture of munitions. It is a very important point in regard to our defence forces. It is necessary not only to organize our military units, not only to buy or manufacture armaments, but also to train in factory practice operations the men who in time of emergency will man the machines and maintain a continuous supply of armaments and munitions.	z

Are young men of to-day willing to learn a trade?
Mr. MacNElL: I assure my hon. friend there are thousands of young men very anxious to get this technical training; witness the experience in the youth training projects. In British Columbia at least I have met many young men who were sorely disappointed because they were not included in the quota selected for the youth training project with regard to technical training, particularly in machine shop practice, acetylene welding, and so on.

Would they not receive training under private enterprise just as well as in government plants?
Mr. MacNElL: The private manufacturer, in order to reduce production costs, hesitates to assume responsibility that would be assumed by government. I am not suggesting that they are unwilling to measure up to their responsibilities, but I am suggesting that they are governed by the interests of their shareholders. They cannot always assume this responsibility.
With regard to the private manufacture of armaments, certain fundamental principles are involved, moral or political, if you like. I think we all desire to escape in Canada the evils which confronted other countries in the private manufacture of armaments. As I have already stated, we have established what amounts to a virtual monopoly in small arms manufacture in Canada. The government have no alternative now but to return, for future orders for munitions and arms of certain calibre, to an established industry where the tooling has been done, where we have practically the only small arms experts in the dominion outside of the departmental offices. That is dangerous. For instance, the firm in question cannot, nor can we expect them to, refuse orders from other sources. True, their operations are subject to the supervision and control of departmental officers, and dominion government orders must have priority, but there may come a time when they must accept orders from abroad, and the moment that happens that unit is hooked up with the international armament ring. That is not at all satisfactory.
May I place on the record the views of certain representative bodies in this regard. There are two well known international organizations of ex-service men, the Confederation Internationale des Associations de Mutiles et

des Anciens Combattants, and the Federation Internationale des Anciens Combattants. Both represent ex-service men all across the world, they have definitely declared themselves on this point. These organizations, which comprise S,000,000 members, adopted the following resolution:
Material disarmament . . . should include the suppression of private manufacture of, and private traffic in, arms, together with effective mutual international control.
There is no longer any doubt as to public opinion in Great Britain on this question. In the peace ballot conducted in 1935, in which some twelve million people voted, this question was asked:
Should the manufacture of and sale of armaments for private profit be prohibited by international agreement?
There was no doubt as to the answer given by the people of Great Britain. Canada is concerned in the decisions of the League of Nations. Under the council of the league there was set up a temporary mixed commission, which had a subcommittee on the private manufacture of armaments composed of representatives of governments, soldiers, sailors, airmen, manufacturers, trade union delegates, economists and civil servants. In its report this statement is included:
It is common knowledge that the public mind is strongly prejudiced against the uncontrolled private manufacture of munitions and implements of war, and that it is a common belief that wars are promoted by the competitive zeal of private armament firms, and would be rendered less frequent were the profit-making impulse brought under control or eliminated altogether. In general the objections that are raised to untrammelled private manufacture may be grouped under the following headings:
(1)	That armament firms have been active in fomenting war scares, and in persuading their own countries to adopt warlike policies and to increase their armaments.
(2)	That armament firms have attempted to bribe government officials both at home and abroad.
(3)	That armament firms have disseminated false reports concerning the military and naval programs of various countries in order to stimulate armament expenditure.
(4)	That armament firms have sought to influence public opinion through the control of newspapers in their own and foreign countries.
(5)	That armament firms have organized international armament rings through which the armaments race has been accentuated by playing off one country against another.
(6)	That armament firms have organized international armament trusts which have increased the price of armaments sold to governments.
I need not read the whole report, but this was a matter of debate in the British House of Commons. Sir John Simon placed a

Supply-National Defence
different construction on it, and in reply, Colonel David Carnegie, the Canadian member of the commission and a leading authority on the subject of armament manufacture, said:
1.	There was no doubt in my mind that the evils enumerated by the sub-committee of the temporary mixed commission regarding the private manufacture of arms were understood to have existed and the subsequent efforts of the temporary mixed commission were directed to prevent such evils from being continued.
2.	Proof of this is found in report A. 16 1924, IX, 30/7/24 where a majority and minority report is given on a draft convention prepared by me and considered by a sub-committee of the temporary mixed commission at Prague. In the minority report the findings of the temporary mixed commission report of September 15th, 1921, are given categorically as an argument for international control.
3.	There can be no doubt whatever that the findings of the sub-committee of the temporary mixed commission determined the scope and nature of the draft convention which I submitted, and during the years I was a member of the temporary mixed commission I do not recollect that any doubt was cast, at least in discussion, as to the correctness of the findings of the sub-committee.
4.	I do not think that the union of democratic control should be condemned for using the word "conclusions," for in my view the members of the temporary mixed commission acted upon them as conclusions; a strong public opinion in the world believed that the evils enumerated existed. If there was any doubt at all then of their existence, which I do not believe, ample proof has been given since that. The findings of the commission have been fully justified.
I quote Mr. Philip Noel-Baker, MP, whose work, The Private Manufacture of Armaments, is accepted almost as a classic. He says:
The nature of this major evil of private manufacture may be stated in the following way;
"The investment of large sums of private capital in armament production creates a permanent and powerful vested interest, the participants in which all depend for their prosperity on the policy which governments pursue in respect of armaments. By the nature of the case, the controlling representatives of this vested interest wield great financial power, are brought by the necessities of their business into close contact with government departments, and generally possess, or are able to establish, close political connections. This vested interest constitutes a powerful force which inevitably favours the increase of armaments and opposes those policies which tend to diminish armaments and reduce the risk of war. It exercises this influence in all important countries in a more or less effective way. Its methods differ according to the political habits and practice of different countries. But. whatever its methods, the effect is the same; the steady pressure of an elaborately organized and financially powerful vested interest against policies which make for peace and in favour of the increase of armaments, whether there is political justification for such increase or not." 71492-261
I think that is a sound basis upon which to approach the question of the private manufacture of armaments, and I can hardly comprehend that there would be any desire in Canada to proceed further in the establishment of vested interests in this country having a heavy investment in the manufacture of war materials. Then we have Admiral Wemyss, for instance, who was first sea lord of the British admiralty, who said that the system of private manufacture-
-is attended by the inevitable consequence that the multiplication of armaments is stimulated artificially.
Lady Wemyss, in writing his biography, and speaking of the last war, said:
For years before its outbreak he had watched the baleful activities of the armament trusts; the manner in which they had, heavily subsidizing the press, influenced public opinion in every country, stirring up strife and creating an atmosphere of hostility, ill will and suspicion between nations.
He had realized all the danger brought about by international rings, who, playing into one another's hands, had a direct interest in the inflation of navy and army estimates and in war scares; for. the more armaments were increased abroad, the more, obviously, had they to foe increased at home.
President Roosevelt of the United States had this to say:
The people of many countries are being taxed to the point of poverty and starvation in order to enable governments to engage in a mad race in armaments, which, if permitted to continue, may well result in war. This grave menace to the peace of the world is due in no small measure to the uncontrolled activities of the manufacturers and merchants of engines of destruction, and it must be met by the concerted action of the peonies of all nations.
And the Premier of France said:
It cannot be doubted, I do not deny it, that there is, in certain countries at least, a temptation for those who manufacture war material and who profit by inflaming conflicts, to perpetuate antagonisms. I believe that we should run fewer risks in future if the world could be wise enough to remove these profits from the daily life of the peoples.
There are many other important statements on this subject, based on the experience of the past. For these important reasons-moral reasons, may I say-the minister should give still further assurance that from now on the government will not overlook the opportunities that present themselves to lay the emphasis on public rather than private manufacture of armaments.

I should like to say just a few words in reference to the item now before the committee. I am afraid the debate, as continued by the hon. member who just sat down, is developing into an argument

Supply-National Defence

against armament manufacture. We have not in Canada any manufacturers coming within the classification of those mentioned by the previous speaker.
We have one now.

During the war Canada produced large quantities o*f many lines of munitions, but as soon as the war was over the companies that had been engaged in that production went out of that business. They broke up lathes which had been specially made for the manufacture of shells, and took out of their plants machines which were unnecessary for the production of the goods they had formerly manufactured. If we had in Canada firms such as were described by the hon. member (Mr. MacNeil), or such as those to which reference has been made by other hon. members, I too would be just as strongly opposed to any company manufacturing implements of war, and through the profits therefrom trying to incite people to acts of violence. But we have not that kind of firm in Canada, and I hope we may never have them. So far as I can see, the argument advanced has no relation to the problem of manufacture in Canada. That type of argument might apply to plants such as the Skoda works in Czechoslovakia.-and I do not say it does. It might apply to the great Creusot works in France; again I do not say it does. But in Canada we have no organization of the kind.
Reference has been made to the small production in the John Inglis plant in Toronto. The production there is insignificant when it is compared with armament production in Europe. After all, 7,000 machine guns is a very small item. Commencing at that point I wish to compliment my leader upon the suggestion he has made, a suggestion which I believe has been endorsed by the minister. Perhaps the minister had the same idea. I do not know about that, but the first I heard of it was when it was mentioned by my leader and by hon. members who have supported him. Each of them deserves praise. I would refer particularly to the hon. members for Vancouver North (Mr. MacNeil) and Vancouver South (Mr. Green) both of whom have endorsed my leader's suggestion. The suggested committee might be described as an inter-party committee of members, and perhaps would be formed so as to include senators. When called together it would try to lay down a definite policy. I have no doubt that in my leader's mind was the thought that by this means we would eliminate from debates in the house discussions such as those we have had through the years- [Mr. MacNicol.J
at least in all the years I have been here- respecting supplies which are necessary for our armed forces. Whether we like it or not, if we are to defend our shores we must have the equipment necessary for that purpose.
The argument is as to whether we should have everything produced in our own arsenals, including the plants at Valcartier and Lindsay, and the John Inglis plant in Toronto, or whether private industry should be called in to assist. I should think the first work of the suggested committee would be to decide upon a definite policy. Having made a decision along that line, as was suggested this morning by the minister, Canada should, as promptly as possible, put itself in a position to defend both eastern and western shores. With my very limited knowledge of these matters I would say that the minister, at the head of the committee, should as quickly as possible assemble the equipment which would be necessary for the defence of our shores. Manifestly all that equipment could not be made in the three arsenals to which I have referred; therefore, at least for the present, private manufacturers would have to be induced to cooperate.
I have no doubt that, under the measure passed some time ago limiting profits in armament manufacture, the minister and officers of his department could prevent any manufacturer from making undue profits. Our defence of the east and west coasts having been attended to, I am satisfied that the Canadian manufacturer would proceed to manufacture his own line making only the profits to which he would be entitled. I doubt whether any of them would remain in the armament business after the orders had been filled. We are not an arms-producing country. Certainly armaments produced in Canada would not be shipped to other parts of the world. The Germans, French, Polish and British could produce their own, and there would be no necessity for the conversion of Canadian plants, such as has been indicated in some of the speeches to which we have listened.
The Canadian manufacturer has given a good account of himself. I have in mind the plant of John T. Hepburn, Limited, located in the constituency of Trinity, Toronto, which is shipping a large number of machines to Australia and Great Britain.
Lathes.

They are shipping high quality lathes to be used in the production of shells. These pieces of machinery are so fine they can be operated by a sixteen-year

Supply-National Defence
old girl. The British government has placed several different orders for these machines, and I believe the Australian government has done likewise. I suppose that machinery would be installed in the private plants about which we have heard. I doubt very much if a government plant would initiate the production of such machinery, because, as some one has pointed out, the profit a private company may get through initiation and development provides an incentive which is not found in the government plant. There is not the same incentive in a government plant to develop or invent.
After we have provided for the defence of our own eastern and western frontiers I believe the government plants could take care of the regular wear and tear and maintain the equipment already built. As I see the problem, cooperation between both suggested plans would ensure the use of our government arsenals to the limit. If necessary we may increase their size, but we should also invite private manufacturers to compete, produce and invent.
Some one has spoken about the plants of the Canadian National Railways. I realize these are first class plants, and that during the war they turned out necessary equipment. I believe shells or munitions of some kind were made in them. Many of the machines used in the plants of the Canadian National Railways were made in Dundas, Ontario. I saw the machines on the floor, ready for shipment and installation. They were manufactured in one of the finest plants on this continent, that of John Bertram and Sons Company, Limited, whose plant is in the constituency of Wentworth. As many as 3,000 men have been employed there at one time. They are inventors; they initiate and produce, and they could supply gun machines required by the government, if they were furnished with blueprints outlining what is desired. I know, too, that there are some first class manufacturing establishments in Brantford. I am familiar with those plants, having been connected with the manufacture of iron and steel products for a great part of my life. Then, in the constituency of Hamilton West-

They
supply much of the machinery for our arsenal at Quebec.

All of these are first class manufacturing establishments, and could be used.
May I express one word of appreciation of what was said by the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin). As I said before, I have felt that perhaps we are parading too much 71492-2614
before the world's gaze our lack of equipment and our inefficiency in methods of defence. It is to be hoped that no bad result may flow from it. On the other hand if we get together, as has been suggested, we might eliminate that parade of conditions before the eyes of the world.
Can we obtain from the United States any of our needs in the way of equipment?

I think we could. Since the imperial conference of 1907 it has been more or less a traditional policy to have our equipment standardized with the designs and patterns of the equipment of the old country. There has been a change in public opinion in this regard, but in the last several months exhaustive inquiries have been made as to the possibility of procurement of certain items in the United States as well as in Great Britain.
Then for all practical purposes there is little hope of our getting any of these requirements from the United States.
That is a difficult question to answer definitely. I feel sure if there were an emergency we could get much equipment from the United States.
To what extent is Canada dependent upon Great Britain for arms and equipment?
I could not give an answer in definite percentages.
Could the minister give us a rough picture of the situation?

Except, for instance; for certain types of heavy guns, modern high angle mountings, certain types of armour-piercing shells, and such things, with proper preparation we could produce most of our requirements in Canada.
Could the minister give us a summary of the orders which have been filled in the last three years in Great Britain for Canada?
Why ask these questions?
I have not that information at hand.
What orders are still unfilled in Great Britain?

I can get that information if my hon. friend wants it, but I should rather give it to him privately.
