With the passing of this item we are committing ourselves to a long-range program with certain features that involve a policy, and unless other arrangements are made for discussing it we have no alternative but to continue the discussion on the item before us.
I am not criticizing the staff officers whose requisitions the minister stated to the committee this morning. I think they have done their duty in stating those requirements. But the committee should have some knowledge as to the strategical objectives in mind and the evidence upon which the staff officers recommend this policy.
The minister mentioned, for instance, 18 destroyers, as being one of the requirements specified by the experts. He made it clear that that has not yet been adopted by the government. But may we know why we are concentrating on destroyers? It is common knowledge that destroyers are expensive, and too fast for convoy work, convoys usually moving at 15 knots and destroyers at a speed of around 35 knots. Further, it is recognized that destroyer flotillas usually operate as units of a battle fleet. Are our destroyer flotillas when finally organized to operate simply as detachments of the British navy, or is their work to be confined strictly to coastal defence? Why is the emphasis placed on destroyers rather than on submarines? A study of naval programs of countries of comparable size to Canada and with a similar coast line shows that emphasis is placed on submarines rather than on destroyers. A submarine can lie in wait at certain points and embarrass a raiding fleet much more effectively than destroyers. Why the emphasis on more destroyers rather than on mosquito craft equipped with detector devices and torpedo firing devices? They also could operate to better advantage in our coastal waters than [DOT] even destroyers.
These are all questions of policy. I am not speaking with the object of having any naval secrets divulged. I am not asking the minister to state publicly in the house what should not be stated publicly, but the strategical objectives could safely be defined without disclosing information that might be of advantage to unfriendly powers. Again, I would ask, why destroyers? Is it the intention of the government to build up a cruiser fleet? A destroyer does not carry guns of heavy enough calibre to enable it to engage a cruiser, which usually carries 6-inch or flinch guns, and should a cruiser raid our coast a destroyer would simply have to stand by. A destroyer, again, is not equipped for transoceanic convoy work but rather for patrol work in the focal areas of our ports. If the
IMr. Roberge.]
minister is unable at this stage to announce his plans with regard to the discussion in committee, could he, for instance, with regard to these long-range features of naval policy and air policy, say something of the strategical objectives which he has in mind, so that we may be assured that they are correlated first of all to Canadian needs?

I wish
to repeat what I said a year ago in this house, that all these estimates are designed for the defence of Canada and only for the defence of Canada. In the second place, in regard to the long-range policy, this vote of S3,000,000 does not in any way affect the long-range policy which was submitted by the general staff to the minister and which I disclosed to the committee this morning. The S3,000,000 concerns only the capital expenditure of $29,000,000 which is part of this year's estimates of $60,000,000, except in so far of course as the $60,000,000 might be considered to be a part of a possible major expenditure.
My hon. friend will recall that I said definitely this morning that the proposed expenditures suggested by the general staff were entirely apart from the estimates of this year

what they thought were adequate for the defence of Canada.
In regard to the proposed committee, I fear it may be somewhat late to set it up formally this year, but if there is a general desire to do so, representatives of the various groups in the house could have an informal meeting, probably next Thursday, call in the chiefs of the staff, and go into the whole question raised by my hon. friend. I would have no objection to holding such a meeting. I thank the minister for the figures he has given. I wish to say just a word or two in support of the argument which has been made by the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. MacNeil) for government ownership of plants for manufacturing military equipment. Canada up to the present time has not been a military country. We have prided ourselves on that fact, and I hope that w'e can maintain this country in the future as a non-military country. But if we are to do that we shall have to consider very carefully military policy within the country, because men engaged in military activities are just the same as people engaged in any other activity- they like to have the thing they are working with as big and as prosperous as possible. That has been found true in other countries where a military caste has got in control. We need only look at the position of Japan, where the military clique is in control, with disastrous results not only to the Japanese people but to other nations as well. We in Canada have to be careful that we do not allow "brass hats" to get control of affairs here. I am afraid it has gone too far already. The government within the last few years has stated definitely that its policy is that so far as possible the manufacture of military supplies and armaments should be carried on in government plants. We are not going to implement that policy by proceeding in an opposite direction. There is only one way to implement a policy, and that is to proceed to put it into effect. The Department of National Defence should explore every possibility, including manufacture in railway shops or any other government shops of materials or equipment or munitions required by this country. I hope, I think we all hope, that this destructive period through which we are passing will be of short duration, that in the not distant future the world will be restored to reason and we shall be able to stop this mad armament race. We should be careful not to be led astray by what is happening in the world to-day and be persuaded to give anybody a free hand or to depart from what has been the policy of this country in the past. I hope that before these estimates pass the committee will satisfy itself that we are not building up an armament interest in this country.
Are any field guns or anti-aircraft guns being manufactured in Canada, or are any plants for their manufacture being established in Canada?
I do not think there are any being manufactured at the present time. Definite plans for the guns are in existence.

I think $36,000,000, in round figures, including all the supplementaries.

Yes. I think it will be found that last year the department was very efficient in spending the amount voted, because in other years the amounts lapsed were two, three or more million dollars. I would estimate that practically all the vote will be spent this year. That is wrhy the word "commitment" is used in the estimate.

I think it would not be in the public interest to answer that question.

I am not in a position to give a definite reply to that question.

Just before one o'clock a question was asked with regard to the utilization of the railway shops for the production of armaments. The minister informed the committee that there was some objection on the part of the management of the shops. I do not know which of the two companies he had in mind, the Canadian National or the Canadian Pacific, but the men who have been writing to me, and probably to other hon. members, in regard to this question, are entitled to some information in that regard. In my own constituency we have a large number of railway employees, in fact one of the largest railway shops in Canada is situated there. To them this is an important question, because at the present time a great many of them are working only about four days a week; in fact the average throughout the year may be even less than that. Would the minister care to elaborate on the statement he made this morning? And will he go even a step farther and inform the committee whether he would care to see what can be done in the matter of the production of armaments in the shops of either or of both railways in different parts of Canada?

All I can say-again I cannot be definite-is that we have complete information in regard to the shops of both railway systems. They have been examined by our inspectors, and we know about their facilities. The trouble is that there has been a certain amount of hesitation-not on the part of the department-in regard to going ahead definitely with any policy in that regard. So far as we are concerned, if the necessity arises we shall be only too glad to cooperate with the railway shops as they would be happy to cooperate with the department.
I understood the minister to say that plans are being made for the manufacture in Canada of field artillery and antiaircraft guns. Is that correct?
We have plans for guns now.
Have any contracts been entered into by the government for the manufacture of either type of equipment?
We have plans with respect to a certain type of gun, but not as to a factory, and no contracts of any kind have been entered into in that regard.

I think the minister misunderstood the question of the hon. member for St. Paul's. What he wanted to find out was whether or not the government are making arrangements to have either anti-aircraft guns or field artillery manufactured in Canada. Could we have that information?

We have ordered a certain number of guns, as I indicated in my address the other day. The question of the production in Canada of one particular type of gun is being carefully and closely investigated. I am not going to discuss guns or calibre here, because I do not think it is in the public interest, but I assure my hon. friend that the department is very much alive to the necessity of having this gun manufactured in Canada if possible.
Are they to come from Canada or Great Britain?
I cannot definitely answer that question.
It is all very well for the minister to be so secretive, but he will remember that there was also a great deal of secrecy about the Bren gun business.

The only point I wish to
make-I have made it before in this house and I do not make it with a view to suggesting that the students are selected on any basis except quality and justice, which I think is certainly the case-is that the Royal Military College is a state-owned institution. In the details of grants to military associations and institutes, the United Service Institutes and the service associations
are listed. What duties do these institutes perform, and have they any bearing on the efficiency of the forces?

Yes. In the first place let me take the service associations-cavalry, artillery, engineers, signals, infantry, machine guns and tanks, army service corps, army medical corps, and a small grant for the Canadian Defence Quarterly. It is about the only organization the nonpermanent militia forces have for the purpose of meeting together and discussing their problems and making representations to headquarters and the officers of the permanent forces. From these various organizations each year there is formed what is called the conference of defence associations. They meet annually in Ottawa, they make representations to the minister and the government, and the president of the conference of defence associations now sits in with the military members of the defence council and discusses various problems affecting particularly the welfare of the non-permanent active militia. My hon. friend is aware of the work which is done by the various institutes. They meet and discuss problems of military importance, and have lectures. Institutes have been established in some of the larger cities of Canada for the purpose of providing a common meeting ground for officers of all arms and militia in the cities and surrounding districts. They are used largely for the purpose of having military lectures and addresses. Not being self-supporting they are assisted with annual grants. Coming to the rifle associations, there are two classes under local rifle associations-military, formed in regiments, squadrons, companies or other units of the service, the Canadian militia and the Royal Canadian Air Force, managed by the officers; and the civilian associations. The active civilian associations are being retained. For some years the policy has been against the formation of any new civilian association, as all available funds are required for the equipment and training of the active permanent and non-permanent units.

I ask that question because the commander of the brigade in Vancouver, Colonel H. F. G. Letson, M.C., whom the minister knows very well, has stated publicly on several occasions that in the militia of British Columbia we have not more than a third of the number of men required to man those forts, and I think something should be done to remedy that situation. understand they are far below it now-or perhaps increase the permanent forces on the coast? At any rate there should be provision for men to man these forts. I should like to know what the department plans to do along that line.

Some

In the general recommendations I mentioned this morning there was a recommendation for an increase in the numbers of the permanent force, but what I think Colonel Letson referred to in the address to which my hon. friend refers was an emergency, and I think he was quite correct when he said that the present strength of the units would not be sufficient to man the coastal fortifications in time of emergency. It is

Earlier to-day the minister said the traditional policy was to standardize on the British type of equipment, and a moment ago he said it was not possible for him to say very much in regard to cooperation with the United States. I can understand that being so for reasons of policy, but I want to take this opportunity to urge upon him the utmost frankness on that point at the earliest possible moment. Our shore lines are, after all, but an extension of the United States shore lines, and people more and more expect definite collaboration. Have we not reached the point when to some extent we should break with tradition, cooperating of course with the British authorities, but quite openly
and frankly exchanging officers with Washington, so far as the United States authorities will permit? In that way we could work out some definite scheme of coastal defence in the interests of both nations. We could get down to brass tacks, and be ready in the event of an emergency confronting both countries. explain why emphasis is put on light machine guns rather than on heavy machine guns. Why should we not have more of the heavy machine guns, rather than the light machine guns?
Supply-National Defence
Why discuss this openly?

The
information I have received-and I think the hon. member referred to it the other day- is that the new light machine gun has replaced the Lewis, and not the Vickers gun. It is capable of sustained fire in an emergency to a much greater degree than the Lewis gun and can, when necessary, be effectively operated by one man. The Vickers gun is still retained in the British army. It is capable of a higher degree of sustained fire than the Bren gun, but requires a larger crew to man it.
The governing factors in the design of a machine gun are power of sustained fire, mobility and crew, no one of which can be satisfied without a corresponding sacrifice of the other two. The difficulty of composing these contradictory factors has resulted in two types of machine gun being adopted for use in the field: the light Bren machine gun with good mobility, the minimum crew and a considerable power of sustained fire; and the medium Vickers machine gun with a very high power of sustained fire but with a corresponding loss in mobility and an increased crew. The Bren gun has been experimented w'ith for a number of years. It has answered all tests and has now been adopted as the universal light machine gun in the British army.
That is the departmental memorandum on the point. Again I would point out I do not claim to be an expert in regard to these matters.

I do not wish to delay my own bill, but perhaps a word of explanation to those who are not members of the railway committee might be in order.
This bill originated, as is noted, in another place, and was reported to this house. Here it was referred to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines. That

Prescott and Ogdensburg Bridge
committee dealt with it and it was reported back with one amendment, which will be reached on section 18. That amendment provides that the company before commencing the bridge must deposit with the government the sum of $50,000 to guarantee completion of construction.

subtopic: PRESCOTT AND OGDENSBURG BRIDGE COMPANY
speechtext:
I should like to find out from the sponsor of this bill whether the Canadian National Railways, who operate in that locality, have considered the policy of claiming this territory for this particular type of bridge. In the first place the national railways have spent a great deal of money in that district. The rapid growth of the motor bus and truck as a competitor of the railways should be considered. No doubt this bill was considered by the senate, but I do not see the Minister of Transport (Mr. Howe) here, and this is an important project. International bridges have been constructed to connect various Ontario points with the United States. Some of these bridges have been a success; some have not. They are taking the business away from the national railways. In the city of Toronto we have the same trouble about the buses and motor-cars; they got control over the situation through the radial entrance. The municipalities should be interested in this. It is a strange thing to me why this bill was introduced in the senate; why did not the proposers of the bill come to the House of Commons which represents the people. What are the views of the municipalities concerned on both sides of the border? What has the state of New York to say about the matter? What control is there over rates? Will this particular type of bridge conform to the Railway Act and be under public regulation on both sides? We have had a great deal of trouble about bridges over the Niagara river. This parliament granted authority for bridges at Sarnia, Windsor, the Niagara river and other places. There should be some public regulation and control and binding action. I do not know anything about this company, but the bill gives it very wide powers. In my opinion the promoters should tell the committee why this bill was introduced in the senate, whether it conforms to the Railway Act and whether Ontario has been consulted and the views of the municipalities on both sides obtained. Will it be necessary to have concurrent jurisdiction with the state of New York?
Since I have been in this parliament we have gone pretty far in incorporating companies for all sorts of purposes, and this bill gives pretty wide powers. It is introduced at

a time when we should give due consideration to whether this parliament should enact bills of this type. I should like to hear from the proposer of the bill.

subtopic: PRESCOTT AND OGDENSBURG BRIDGE COMPANY
speechtext:
I have to voice my opposition to this bill on a number of grounds. It is not my intention to delay third reading, but I wish to draw the attention of the committee to three or four main reasons which I believe are paramount against the passing of this bill.
The first is that when a bridge is about to be constructed in any city, town or municipality there should be traffic congestion. If there is no traffic congestion then, generally speaking, there is no necessity for a bridge. In the standing committee this afternoon we were given a number of details relative to that question. My submission is that there is no traffic congestion at Prescott, at any rate not a sufficient amount to warrant the construction of this bridge. On the contrary the figures indicate just the opposite. In 1937 some 55.000 vehicles crossed at Prescott; in 1938, only 47,000.

subtopic: PRESCOTT AND OGDENSBURG BRIDGE COMPANY
speechtext: Yes, on a ferry.

subtopic: PRESCOTT AND OGDENSBURG BRIDGE COMPANY
speechtext:
Yes, on a ferry. So that, assuming the bridge to be constructed, and comparing that position at Prescott with the present position at Ivy Lea, one certainly would not have double the number of cars going in and coming out that one has at the present time. And if the same condition that at present exists at Ivy Lea were to exist at Prescott, this financial expenditure is not warranted. We were told this morning that the cost of the bridge would be in the neighbourhood of $3,200,000. Even if you had 100,000 cars crossing the bridge at, say $1 each, it would not give enough return to pay the operating expenses, let alone the interest on the bonds.
There is another objectionable feature, namely, that there are already too many bridges along the St. Lawrence river. At the present time there are four such bridges between Montreal and Niagara Falls; one at Caughnawaga, one at Cornwall, one at Ivy Lea, and the Niagara Falls bridge.
Unfortunately all the capital in these undertakings is United States. I do not mean that we should not welcome United States capital in this country; but the moment the Americans are incorporated under United States authority they buy the Canadian charter, as they did at Brockville and as they probably will do at Prescott, and then they take control of the Canadian side. I wish to register strong opposition to that angle of the case.

Prescott mid Ogdcnsburg Bridge
There is another feature, namely, that this country should sooner or later realize the importance of public ownership of these schemes, as exists at the present time in the United States. When that comes, there may also follow what we all expect, freedom from tolls. I believe that is the ultimate end that the United States authorities have in mind. But so far as Canada is concerned we are doing this business entirely through Canadian corporations; private companies are being set up, and they are being purchased by United States concerns. The result is that United States capitalists take full control of these bridges. I say also that if this bridge is constructed the door is open to anyone who may wish to apply for a similar charter. At the present time there are ferries at points all along the St. Lawrence between Montreal and Windsor. At some places the traffic is not nearly as heavy as it is at Prescott, while at other places it is heavier. Probably next year or the year after those people will come here demanding similar powers.
There is only one redeeming feature in the bill, namely, the amendment which was made this afternoon in the railway committee, which stipulates that before any work is done in connection with the scheme, the sum of $50,000 must be deposited by the United States company as a guarantee.
For these reasons, Mr. Chairman, I am opposed to this bill.

speechtext:
I am in favour of the bill because of the conditions under which we are presently operating. But as I had occasion to point out to the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines this morning, I would draw to the attention of the government the desirability of setting up in Canada a commission or a public body empowered to deal wirt these international bridges. This bridge will have no capital, so to speak. It has only five hundred dollars made up of five qualifying shares for its directors. When the bonds to

Prescott and Ogdensburg Bridge
be issued will have been redeemed out of the earnings of the bridge, the bridge will be turned over, that part of it lying within the United States to the government of the state of New York, and that part of it lying within Canada to the government of Canada. It will then become a public bridge.
It has been necessary to create this corporation to carry out the project, because we have no such body presently existing in Canada. Within the last nine or ten years several international bridges have been built, but there is no uniformity of regulation and legislation in connection with them. We have the board of transport commissioners who have power to regulate the bridge, so far as the safety of the public is concerned, the proper operation of the bridge, the regulation of traffic and tolls.

subtopic: PRESCOTT AND OGDENSBURG BRIDGE COMPANY
speechtext:
Why should it not be placed under the jurisdiction of the international
waterway commission?

subtopic: PRESCOTT AND OGDENSBURG BRIDGE COMPANY
speechtext:
It might very well be placed under the jurisdiction of that body. But the international waterway commission deals more with international waters than with bridges. But I would see no insuperable difficulty in adding to their powers whereby they would be able to operate under authority of a bill of this kind.
I believe the time has come when such a body should be set up, either in the form of a new commission or, as has been suggested, by adding to the powers of the international waterway commission. I take this opportunity to draw the attention of the government to the desirability of passing uniform legislation and setting up an authority capable of dealing with matters of this kind. Further I think it would be good business for this country to enter into an agreement with the government of the United States or of the state of New York to redeem all bonds presently outstanding in connection with all international bridges, and at the earliest possible moment to make them free. I believe any money spent in that direction would be more than repaid by the great incentive it would give to the tourist traffic which has become one of our Canadian industries.

What is the matter with that thing now?
There are four main reasons, Mr. Speaker, why this bill should pas. The first one is that it would give employment to a lot of our fishermen, many of whom are on relief or pretty close to it. Secondly, it would promote the conservation of fish, something that is badly needed now, because if the traps are allowed to continue the salmon fishing will disappear. The third is the big loss that will come to us on this side of the line by our not taking out our traps, thus encouraging the Americans to put theirs back in. We have only five, while they had 219, and they are threatening to put them back in because we do not take our five out, in consequence of a gentleman's agreement made on both sides of the line. When their traps went out our share of the Fraser river catch rose from 30 to 86 per cent, and the total catch went down. So there is that advantage; it saves the run of fish by catching less fish, while our fishermen caught much more. The fourth reason is that if our traps are continued there it will mean the loss of our splendid naval reserve of fishermen. If our trapping goes on, the Americans having taken theirs out, they will put back their traps, and in a short time 90 per cent of our fishing will disappear and 90 per cent of our fishermen who go to make up the naval reserve will also disappear. Trained fishermen cannot be found at a moment's notice. The coast is honeycombed by propaganda and by fishermen from a foreign nation. Our fishermen know all that coast and acting as pilots, scouts, mine layers, et cetera, would be invaluable; they would almost be worth their weight in gold. For that work they would be better than a man off a warship. We have already started a naval reserve there with two hundred of our young fishermen, the
finest God ever put breath into. What are you going to do in time of war if you take away the livelihood of these men? You do not get much loyalty or protection in time of war from a collection of piles and a lot of wire-netting.
To take up the various points, fishing by means of traps is admittedly the most destructive form of fishing, and if allowed to go on it will destroy the industry. Alaska has already struck hundreds of them out, and British Columbia has stopped them all except five or six at Sooke. The United States stopped them and took out 219 traps at Puget sound, on the gentleman's understanding that we would do the same. The trap net is to fishing what a pump gun is to a man going out shooting. Why is it not allowed? Because you would kill off the ducks. And why should trap fishing be allowed? You are not allowed to use a machine gun to shoot deer. Mankind is the only victim that you are allowed to slaughter indiscriminately. You cannot use the roe of salmon when fishing for trout because the trout would soon disappear. The fishermen are asking that they be not allowed to use sole as bait for cod. Why? Because it is so effective that the cod banks would soon disappear. It is the same principle with the trap.
As regards the results on the United States side, they had 219 traps. The fish come round by Sooke and into Puget sound. They were decimated by these 219 traps. Then they come to the Fraser river to breed and spawn. But the moment the Americans took out their traps-they never could get the measure through the legislature, and it was done on the initiative of the people in the state of Washington-that moment the catch on the Fraser river ran up from 30 to as high as 86 per cent of the whole. For two years the vested interests tried to put a repeal measure through their legislature, but without success. They almost got the measure through last year; they got it through the upper house but not through the lower. What is one of the arguments that have been adduced? It is this: "Perfidious Albion has not played the game; we took our traps out, but Canada has not done so, so let us put our traps back in again." A very plausible argument. If we do not take our traps out, the argument will be too strong against us the next time the matter comes up. If we do not take ours out, it will be a splendid argument for those on the United States side to put theirs back in again. We have only five traps, and if you took them out

it would give employment to about two hundred or more men. That is worth something.
If we leave the traps in and the Americans put theirs back in again, we lose our fishermen for the naval service. We decided to take out the traps all over British Columbia except at Sooke, and only allowed them there because on the United States side they had 219 traps. But we did not allow them anywhere else, and when they asked for traps elsewhere in the north we said, "No, but we must let them have them at Sooke, because of these particular conditions." If we do not take the traps out now, the cannerymen, standing by, will say, "If you allow traps in one place you will have to allow them all over British Columbia." The argument will be logical and we shall find it hard to refuse. Once allow that, and it will be a very short time before ninety per cent of the fishermen will disappear; for only ten per cent of the present number will be required as trap tenders, and after that the fishing industry will go down too. That is why it is so vital and important that we should take this step now.

On all these counts upon which I have touched I submit we should pass this bill. The people of British Columbia are aroused. I presented a petition of 10,000 last year and one of the 2,500 this year. But that is not so outstanding. The associated boards of trade of Vancouver island, last year, after a desperate attempt by the trap owners to get this resolution rescinded, passed, after a three-hour debate, a resolution confirming their former action and again turned down the trap owners. The Vancouver board of trade are not fools, nor are the city councils of Vancouver and New Westminster, or the Prince Rupert board of trade, or the Prince Rupert town council, or the Trades and Labour councils. Are they all so gullible? People quite remote from the particular interests concerned are taking an interest in this and are determined to get action, although they are not directly affected. I hold in my hand a communication which came to me two nights ago. Talk of me "railroading" stuff; I did not know that this body was in existence. The Vancouver youth council, at a recent congress attended by 232 delegates-almost as many as the members of this house-and representing 45,113 young people, put on record a very strong resolution along the lines I have indicated, and they end up with these words:
This is the considered opinion of the young people of this province, and the outcome of the present debate will be watched with considerable interest.
The population of British Columbia is not large, and when one finds 45,000 young people taking such a keen interest in this matter it shows that the people generally are on the alert. In this case it is not a question of a

one-man fight. There are seven members from British Columbia concerned in this matter, and only two of them are in favour of the traps; the other five are against them, and almost everybody who knows this subject and who is not directly interested in the traps takes that view. British Columbia is aroused on the subject, and I predict that those men who support traps will not come back to this house after the next election. If my constituents who have been so kind and so loyal to me over the years should honour me again, I shall associate myself with men of like minds and we shall not let the thing die, we shall carry it on. I will support no government and no party which approves fish traps. They are a relic of the feudal system. Thirty years ago one man would control fifty or one hundred square miles of water and one could not put a hook or net or line into that water without his permission. It was the feudal system gone riot, and this is a foul remnant which has not been wiped out. We have now an open policy so that a man does not have to go to a cannery to get permission to fish.

subtopic: SUPERVISION OVER STOCKYARD OPERATIONS- GRADING, INSPECTION AND MARKETING
speechtext:
When this bill was before the house on first and second reading there was little or no discussion on it. The minister stated at that time that it was to go before the standing committee on agriculture, and for that reason I believe hon. members refrained from saying anything. The bill went before the agriculture committee and was passed practically in the form in which it was introduced into the house.
This is a new bill, as we were given to understand in committee, yet it incorporates very largely the features of the bill of 1923.
Live Stock and Poultry

It also incorporates, I believe, a number of regulations which were in force under that bill. The bill was somewhat hard to follow in committee because there were very few explanatory notes. It was explained at that time that explanatory notes are never printed in a new bill. But this bill is, after all, a revival of the bill of 1923 with a number of the regulations and some added features. It would have been much easier to follow if there had been explanatory notes showing which clauses are new and which are old.
There are three parts to this bill:	The
first deals with stockyards and operations within them; the second, with live stock and live stock products, particularly grading and marketing, and the third, with hatcheries.
In the main I am fully in accord with the provisions of the bill. I believe it goes a long way to assist agriculture in its marketing problems. But I believe some things that have been omitted from the bill might very well have received more consideration and some day will be incorporated into legislation, because, if they are, it will give the department more authority than they have at the present time.
The first feature of the bill which is new is the appointment of an advisory committee. There have been advisory committees set up in other branches of the Department of Agriculture, in the seed branch, and there is a bill before the house to appoint an advisory committee to deal with cheese and the dairy industry. This is a good feature, if it is properly carried out. But if it is going to be successful and fulfil the purpose for which it is intended, the committee must be fully representative of all live stock interests, both producers' organizations and distributing agencies. Of course that will depend largely upon the minister himself, who will give authority to different organizations to appoint members. There is no statement in the bill as to how many members this advisory committee will comprise. Perhaps the minister will inform us what he has in mind in that regard.
Part I, as I said, deals with stockyards and operations within the stockyards; and there is a new feature in this, because the bill assumes some control over packers' yards as well as public stockyards. One feature of part I of which I doubt the efficacy is that the power to control and set up regulations and fees and charges has been taken away from the live stock exchanges and given to the stockyard companies, that is the companies which own and control the stockyards. The reason 
assigned by the minister for doing this is that there are, I think he said, eleven stockyards and only six live stock exchanges within those yards. In those stockyards which are owned and operated by railway companies and by Canadian interests I have no fault to find with the new set-up. But at least one stockyard company I know of is largely controlled by foreign capital, and I am not sure but I think it is true that certain packers' interests have at least some control of some of the other stockyards, controlling interests in some of the stockyard companies. If this be true, it would be unwise to vest such power and authority in these stockyard companies, particularly unless strict supervision over the arrangements they make is undertaken by the department itself.
So far as the control assumed in this bill over packers' yards is concerned, it is all to the good. As years go by an increasing amount of our live stock is marketed in packers' yards rather than in the public stockyards, and it is high time that the power which this bill gives should be taken by the department to control in some way not only the construction and equipment but the management of packers' yards. I shall mention only one thing, something that is very much talked about among producers, and which I hesitate to mention; it is this, that in the public stockyards the weighmasters are appointed and paid by the companies. The packers or whoever buy animals in those stockyards have no interest in the weighing; it is controlled by weighmasters appointed by someone else. But when cattle or hogs' go into the packers' yards they are weighed by weighmasters who are in the employ of and paid by the packing companies. I am not suggesting at the moment that there is any dishonesty there, but I say that if neutral weighmasters could be appointed, or someone who is in a neutral position-I would even go so far as to say someone appointed by the department-placed in a position of weighing the live stock that comes into these packers' yards, in the same way as grain is weighed under the grain act, this would at least remove from the minds of the producers any suspicion of wrongdoing. I urge the minister to consider that matter carefully.
Another point is that if the owners of the stockyards are to set up the regulations and the fees and charges they will, practically speaking, control the commission men who operate on those exchanges. It is undoubtedly true that, in some instances at least, there are too many commission firms operating in

Live Stock and Poultry
the different yards. Of course the argument will be advanced that the more commission men there are, the more competition there is in the market. If there is scarcity on the market I believe that the more commission men there are, the better. But when there is a surplus of cattle, more than can be disposed of, I do not think competition enters into the matter at all. And unfortunately, if there are too many men operating on any particular market, I believe there is a tendency to raise the fees too high in order that they can all exist.
There is another matter, not dealt with in this bill, which I think requires serious consideration. I refer to the necessity of some kind of control over truckers. During the last few years, particularly in Ontario, a large business has grown up in the shipment of hogs and cattle to the yards of the packers and to the stockyards by means of trucks. In many instances the trucker himself operates as a commission man or dealer, assuming the same powers that are assumed by commission men on the market. The regular commission men, however, are provided with concise and complete forms on which to make their returns to the men who consign cattle or hogs to them. They must keep special bank accounts; they must make government deposits to assure those who deal with them that they are in no danger whatever of losing money. I think the day is not far distant when this or some other government will have to take this matter in hand, because, as time goes on, it is becoming much more of a business, and I believe it will continue to increase.
I want to say just one more word and then I have finished for the present, although I may have something further to say as some of the sections come up for consideration. Part 2 of the bill provides for the control and regulation of exports; I believe that will be found in section 34 or 35. I am strongly of opinion that the control over the quantity and quality of our exports has not been sufficiently stringent. I have made the statement on more than one occasion in this house that I believe that situation exists particularly in connection with cheese and bacon. As I have stated previously, we have the grain act under which the quality of our grain going to the United Kingdom and other foreign markets is always carefully supervised. I believe it is right that this should be so. I sat in the agriculture committee during the revision of the grain act during the last week or two, and I heard a great deal about control samples and all the rest of it. I believe that is the
right system to follow. In the case of bacon going to the mother country, in my judgment we have altogether too many grades. To-day Canadian bacon is about ten shillings per long hundredweight below Danish bacon on the English market. That is altogether too great a difference; and if it is true, as has been stated many times, that the price we receive for Canadian bacon in the British market is one of the principal factors controlling the price of hogs in Canada, then I think the higher the price we get for our bacon in England, the better it will be for the hog industry and, in fact, the whole live stock industry. I would urge upon the minister and his officials that they tighten up the regulations, particularly in connection with allowing packers and shippers to send so many different grades of bacon to the old country market.

There is a tremendous difference in the weights of hogs or cattle. What is commonly known as off-car weights receive one price, while fed-and-watered rates receive another price in the daily market quotations. The situation in Canada in that regard, as the minister knows, also obtains in Chicago, Buffalo, St. Louis, St. Paul and all the other United States markets, where we get our lead. With the advent of the truck, however, which is so rapidly taking the place of carload lots, the old rules in regard to the difference in weight as between off-car weight in the one instance and fed-and-watered weight in the other, no longer obtain. Trucks travel as far as two hundred miles to bring live stock of all kinds to market, but has the government inspector any opportunity of ascertaining whether any particular load of live stock has travelled that distance without feed and water? They have no background of experience on which they can base their judgment, and I believe those charged with the administration of this legislation, who will receive their instructions from this advisory committee, should give special study to that feature of it, so that the producer may get a fair deal when his live stock are weighed up.

The committee will be called in, and will advise in connection with activities in the country. The department will be guided by the advice it receives from the committee, but the instructions will largely come from the department.

subtopic: SUPERVISION OVER STOCKYARD OPERATIONS- GRADING, INSPECTION AND MARKETING
speechtext:
The department, according to what the minister has just said, will be guided by the instructions it receives from the committee. As I understand the situation, it is the duty of the minister to see to it that producers and live stock organizations are listened to by his department, and also see to it that the Department of Agriculture is not in any way dominated by the packing house industry. No one in the live stock industry knows as much about the operation of the live stock branch of the department as do those who are engaged in the packing house industry. As the minister knows, they have their men here on each and every occasion, when any little matter arises. The producer organizations in Canada are not properly organized. To my mind they do not have a representation of a kind which gives continuous attention to the industry, so far as the relationship of the industry to the department is concerned. From my observations in the last fifteen years there has not been the same connection between producers and the department as there has been between packing house interests and the department. That is a weakness on the part of live stock producers associations.
The live stock producers of Canada are not headed up sufficiently to approach not only this but other problems affecting them. I feel that in a committee such as is here suggested the producers of live stock in this country should be given proper recognition. The minister will say at once that they are getting every recognition, but I would point out to him that they do not have what is commonly described by the men on the street as lobbyists, economists or any personnel of that kind close to the heads of the Department of Agriculture. To my mind they are not sufficiently close to give proper consider-
Live Stock and Poultry
ation to this and all other legislation affecting the live stock producers, whereas the organizations which receive the live stock are highly organized. They are listened to by the deputy minister. And much of the legislation in the last twenty-five years which has come before committees such as this has been legislation which was reviewed and put up by the deputy minister to the minister holding office at the time. But prior to that it has been lobbied for and asked for by highly organized interests in this country-and of course it is well that we have well organized packing houses. At the same time a little more balance in the equation on behalf of the producers of live stock would not go amiss.

subtopic: SUPERVISION OVER STOCKYARD OPERATIONS- GRADING, INSPECTION AND MARKETING
speechtext:
What would be the
duties of the proposed committee, and would it operate continuously or only be called in from time to time by the department?

subtopic: SUPERVISION OVER STOCKYARD OPERATIONS- GRADING, INSPECTION AND MARKETING
speechtext:
It would be similar to the committee which operates under the seed branch. That is, there would be a committee representative of live stock unions and producers from across Canada who would be called in. When they are called in, their expenses would be paid. They would not be under any obligation to pay expenses in connection with trips they would make when advice is sought from them. The objective of having a committee of this kind is to meet the very kind of criticism to which the hon. member for Danforth has called attention. It goes without saying that packing plants across Canada do see to it that their ideas with regard to trading are kept constantly before the department. There is no doubt about that, and one would expect it, because the packing plants are well organized. They are equipped to have men available at all times to come to the department and make representations on their behalf. There is no doubt that they have always made those representations. The question as to the extent to which they influence officials in the department or legislation passing through the department may be an entirely different matter. But it is only natural to suppose that when the public see men associated with the packing houses constantly coming to Ottawa, and see reports in the press that those representatives have been here to make representations, they are inclined to place perhaps too much emphasis upon the influence that those men may have.
In order to guard against that kind of thing the suggestion is that we have an advisory committee, that men be appointed representing other interests in the live stock industry, and that those men be permitted to come to Ottawa to place their case before the government from time to time. As a matter of fact that is why in the early part of the discussion I was not too definite in stating that the packing houses would be represented on this committee. At the moment I am not absolutely convinced that there is a necessity for any strong representation, if any, on the part of the packing houses. From time to time they do come here and make their representations. It is just possible it might be desirable to have all parts of the industry meet from time to time in a committee of this kind in order that the representations of all parties may be known to one another. I speak of representations in connection with legislation, or activities of the department.
But I would say that there is no doubt whatever that, apart from the packing plants, all other interests in the industry will be represented on the committee. It is just possible, too, that it may be thought advisable to have a small representation from the packing houses on the same committee.

subtopic: SUPERVISION OVER STOCKYARD OPERATIONS- GRADING, INSPECTION AND MARKETING
speechtext: Will the advisory committee have anything to do with, for instance, the setting of the price differential on bacon hogs- heavies, lights and so on? Perhaps at the same time the minister could tell the committee who sets the differential now between selects, heavies and lights?

subtopic: SUPERVISION OVER STOCKYARD OPERATIONS- GRADING, INSPECTION AND MARKETING
speechtext: I cannot accept that answer, that it is the market which sets the differential. I believe the next sentence was more to the point. But who decides the difference?

speechtext: There may be some criticism of the way in which the market is set, but whatever market we have, it really sets the differential. The packer makes his bid, and whoever owns the live stock has the choice whether or not he accepts. It is quite possible that he has not much choice if there is no other place in which to sell.

subtopic: SUPERVISION OVER STOCKYARD OPERATIONS- GRADING, INSPECTION AND MARKETING
speechtext:
The market starts on Monday morning with a certain price, depending upon the shortage or over-run in all parts of Canada and the United States, but in this instance there is a fixed differential between
Live Stock and Poultry

selects, lights and feeders and bacon hogs. That differential obtains month in and month out, week in and week out.

subtopic: SUPERVISION OVER STOCKYARD OPERATIONS- GRADING, INSPECTION AND MARKETING
speechtext: I have before me a statement of the markets and the differentials, and I would suggest that it does not bear out the claim just made. It does not indicate that there is anything really set about it. I find the Toronto market on April 27 shows lights and feeders selling at a discount of $1.50. In the Montreal market lights and feeders averaged a price of $9.10, while bulk sales were from $9 to $9.25. There is a difference all the way through the market. On the Winnipeg market bacon hogs were selling at $785, and lights and feeders at $8. That is just a fair indication that the market has something to do with setting the differential. What is being offered and what is being demanded on a particular day does set the differential.

subtopic: SUPERVISION OVER STOCKYARD OPERATIONS- GRADING, INSPECTION AND MARKETING
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when a
carload of mixed hogs arrive at the market, it is well known that the packer will take the whole carload or none at all, and he fixes his price on that basis. Selects get a premium, while heavies are forced to take a certain deduction, but the owner of the hogs or the shipper has no choice. He cannot sell his lights to the special buyer referred to a moment ago by the minister. This is one of the matters about which the producers of hogs in this country complain justly. It is not right to say that the market fixes the price of hogs. For instance, the Montreal market generally runs to heavies, but if we have a carload of hogs made up of heavies, bacons, lights and others, the packer says he will take all or none. The shipper knows very well that if he takes out the selects or the lights or the heavies he will not be able to sell the others so easily. The packer gets the carload for the carload run.
Under this section the minister proposes to set up an advisory committee. I think this is a good thing, but it will not only be worse than useless, it will be just another nail in the producers coffin if this advisory committee is dominated by the packers as is the whole situation to-day. I have no desire to reflect on the packers, but it must be as clear as daylight that the disorganized or individual producer cannot compete with the organized packers. The minister has stated that occasionally the packers come to Ottawa, but last year I asked for a return of the correspondence between his department and the Canadian packers and Mr. Todd. What was the result?

subtopic: SUPERVISION OVER STOCKYARD OPERATIONS- GRADING, INSPECTION AND MARKETING
speechtext: He is the secretary of the whole group.

subtopic: SUPERVISION OVER STOCKYARD OPERATIONS- GRADING, INSPECTION AND MARKETING
speechtext:
What was the result? The minister's own officials rang me up and asked me not to insist on their bringing down that correspondence. My motion was for a limited time, I believe for two or three years, but they told me there was a ton of it. They offered to send over the index, and they sent me several boxes containing hundreds of index cards. It was quite obvious that there were several hundred files. I looked through the index, and I discovered that there was not even a minute regulation passed in the live stock branch which was not referred to Toronto. There was case after case, and evidence that day after day the officials of the department were running to Toronto to consult these people. The minister talks about the packers coming to Ottawa occasionally and exercising a little influence, but this is what the files showed. Let me repeat, so long as the packing industry dominates the live stock branch in the way it has for the last fifteen years, the farmer of this country will never receive a fair deal.
A moment ago I asked what was in this bill to protect the producer of live stock, but so far as I can find out from the bill, there is virtually nothing. The minister has said something about inspectors going into the packing plants, but that does not amount to a snap of one's fingers.

subtopic: SUPERVISION OVER STOCKYARD OPERATIONS- GRADING, INSPECTION AND MARKETING
speechtext: There is a great deal that we cannot regulate from here.

subtopic: SUPERVISION OVER STOCKYARD OPERATIONS- GRADING, INSPECTION AND MARKETING
speechtext:
There is a great deal that can be regulated from Ottawa. What happens? A truckload of hogs is driven up to a packing plant, and in the majority of instances the trucker, who is the trustee of the farmer, backs up his truck and sits in his seat while the packing house employees weigh and grade the load and do everything else with the hogs. The trucker takes the ticket that is given to him. If I were to suggest that they were not giving the farmer a square deal, I suppose I would be charged with saying that the packers were not honest. That is not the question at all. A fundamental law in trading is the law that states that the fellow who buys should not also be the seller. The man who is doing the selling should have a chance to check his weights, classifications and prices. I venture to say that not ten per cent of the farmers shipping live stock by truck to-day are ensured a square deal, human nature being what it is. There are

Live Stock and Poultry
some stories going round as to what happens in connection with these unsupervised weighings, but I have not been able to verify these.
I am told there are things going on that ought to be stopped, and I may tell the minister that his officials know that these things ought to be stopped.

speechtext: I do not think the hon. gentleman should be allowed to go on in this way discussing section 13. If we are going to discuss this particular matter in the manner in which it is being discussed, then I insist on its being discussed in its proper place, and that is not on section 8.

I would call the

They are largely marketed twice a year, because the litters come twice a year and in six months are ready for market. Just at the time they are being sold, the packer or someone in control of the situation forces the price down, but the instant the hogs are out

of the farmers' hands, up goes the price again. Yet the bacon from these hogs is all sold at the same price. Whether the price for hogs is high or low, the bacon sells at the same price. speechtext:
I was challenged a few moments ago as being out of order, but I

cannot allow this section to pass in silence. This is a live stock measure; it deals with live stock and live stock products. There are two sides to the marketing of live stock- the producers' side and the buyers' side. The two sides are absolutely distinct, and are in conflict one with the other. It is not fair to the producers of the country to set up an advisory committee that will be dominated by the packers. I suggest to the minister that the advisory committee be composed exclusively of producers. The minister could have his processing committee on the other side if he wishes, and bring the two together round a table under the chairmanship of himself or someone else in the department, but there should be a committee or advisory board composed of producers and producers only. Their interest is in direct conflict with that of the packers or processors, and so long as the packers or processors are on the committee they will dominate it. They are doing that very thing to-day, and they have done it for fifteen years.

subtopic: SUPERVISION OVER STOCKYARD OPERATIONS- GRADING, INSPECTION AND MARKETING
speechtext: There need be no fear that a committee of the kind proposed here would be dominated by the packers. As a matter of fact I am not at all sure that there will be packers on it, but I would not care to commit the department or any minister who may be in charge of it, myself or anyone else, by saying that the packers never would be represented on a committee of this kind.

subtopic: SUPERVISION OVER STOCKYARD OPERATIONS- GRADING, INSPECTION AND MARKETING
speechtext: Why not separate the two functions?

subtopic: SUPERVISION OVER STOCKYARD OPERATIONS- GRADING, INSPECTION AND MARKETING
speechtext: There might be an argument for separating them in the same way as we separate those interested in hogs and those interested in poultry, but I can conceive of its being essential sometimes that both sides of the activities in connection with the industry be brought together, and it is just possible it will be necessary to have meeting after meeting, where the packers and also the producers will be represented. I cannot conceive of any meeting being held at which, if the producers are represented by the type of men whom I have usually found representing producers in different parts of Canada, they would be dominated very much by anyone. Just as able men will be found among the producer organizations of this country as are in the packing plants.

subtopic: SUPERVISION OVER STOCKYARD OPERATIONS- GRADING, INSPECTION AND MARKETING
speechtext:
I should like to say a word along that line. Last year I attended a successful show of pure-bred swine, and on one of the nights the show was going on, a number of producers, including men
Live Stock and Poultry
prominent in the swine industry in Canada as well as in the province in which the show was located, met with a representative of the packers-I do not recall his name; I never met him before-and discussed matters of mutual interest. At the close of that conference, which was entirely informal, the leading swine producers there expressed themselves as having learned more about various problems which had been troubling them than they had ever known before, although they were not in entire agreement with the packers' representative. They came to a better understanding, for instance, of the British swine regulations, whereunder the price is based largely on the cost of feed, and the government tried to set up a price for bacon which would enable the farmer to pay for his feed and his labour and show some little profit when his product was marketed. In connection with that they pointed out that it would likely happen this year that prices would be lower because of the lower cost of feed in the old country. This, of course, is true in Canada as well, and permits the making of a profit on bacon sold at a somewhat lower price. They also pointed out something which I am sure most producers would not recognize, and which I have never heard discussed in this chamber, namely, the fact that the difference in exchange between British money and our money last fall, varying from around $4.90 to S4.70-and the spread may have been a little wider than that-meant a difference of about half a cent a pound on the live hog. That is something well worth knowing in order to remove a feeling that injustice is being done when the reason for such a difference is not apparent.
Another point which was of great interest to many swine producers last year was the high price which ruled up to about August and the heavy drop which took place after that date, a drop which was greater than normal. It was indicated that last year packers in western Canada had to bring in pork products from Ontario to hold their own domestic market because on account of lack of feed in the crop of 1937, many producers had gone out [DOT]of business for the time being and there was not enough stuff on the western markets to supply the demand. The home demand had to be met at all costs, so for the first time in many years pork products went west instead of coming east as they usually have done.
With reference to something the minister touched upon at the close of his last remarks, I should like to say that the men who represented the producers were just as keen, perhaps keener, and more alert in many ways, than the representatives of any packers could
be. Certainly they were just as keen, but they had not had some particular points brought to their attention before. They expressed themselves as well satisfied with the conference and anxious to have similar conferences from time to time. They were of opinion that it was a valuable experience to them to meet representatives of other branches of the industry such as the packers. I do not mean that they agreed with regard to everything. I do not suppose a board such as is to be set up now, if it includes packers' representatives and producers' representatives, will always get along quite smoothly. But I do say it will be a good thing to have them coming together at times to thresh out problems of common interest.

subtopic: SUPERVISION OVER STOCKYARD OPERATIONS- GRADING, INSPECTION AND MARKETING
speechtext:
It seems to me that the
remarks of the hon. member for Melfort serve entirely to prove the contention of the hon. member for Kootenay East. subtopic: SUPERVISION OVER STOCKYARD OPERATIONS- GRADING, INSPECTION AND MARKETING
speechtext:
I should like to ask the hon. member for Haldimand whether it would not be better for the producers to thresh out these points with the representatives of any other branch of the industry in order to get what information they may have to offer them-tested and tried, if you like; I do not suppose they would accept it unthinkingly-before making their final representations to the department, so that they
Live Stock and Poultry

can have all the information they can get, from whatever source it comes.

subtopic: SUPERVISION OVER STOCKYARD OPERATIONS- GRADING, INSPECTION AND MARKETING
speechtext: I suppose it is to the minister rather than to me that the question should be addressed, but I would say that is the very job which is up to the officials of the department, to keep themselves posted on these matters and not to be influenced in any way by extraneous considerations. speechtext:
I agree that is
so. The men from the farms have certainly the ability and the native intelligence, but there are points upon which they are not informed. subtopic: SUPERVISION OVER STOCKYARD OPERATIONS- GRADING, INSPECTION AND MARKETING
speechtext: That is what the departmental officials are there for.

subtopic: SUPERVISION OVER STOCKYARD OPERATIONS- GRADING, INSPECTION AND MARKETING
speechtext: It is not exactly what they are there for. The function of the departmental officials is two-fold. They are interested in the producing end and they are interested in organization and marketing.

subtopic: SUPERVISION OVER STOCKYARD OPERATIONS- GRADING, INSPECTION AND MARKETING
speechtext: Look at the next clause and see.

subtopic: SUPERVISION OVER STOCKYARD OPERATIONS- GRADING, INSPECTION AND MARKETING
speechtext: But I do not think it would be reasonable to expect that they would be as aware as are the packers of changes in the market from day to day, the difficulties of marketing, and the true inwardness of various matters affecting the market in the old country, unless a special organization were built up for that purpose. speechtext:
It is bound to be an organization of a different type from that which the packers must have in order to

preserve their very lives. Government agencies generally, while they are useful and gather information, are not of the same type and are not actually engaged in the business.

subtopic: SUPERVISION OVER STOCKYARD OPERATIONS- GRADING, INSPECTION AND MARKETING
speechtext: This section is really a new feature. It was not in previous legislation, and it meets to some extent the requests and desires of all members of the committee. I agree with the suggestion made by my hon. friend opposite. I certainly would hope that the committee would be set up in such a way that it would not be dominated by the organized meat packing industry or the organized elements of the industry. The only thing I thought of comparing it with at the moment was the committee set up under the Seed Act, whereon both producers and representatives of the industry itself compose that committee; and I assume they hold meetings occasionally to deal with the matters of mutual interest. I understood it was the same feature largely being incorporated in this section.

subtopic: SUPERVISION OVER STOCKYARD OPERATIONS- GRADING, INSPECTION AND MARKETING
speechtext:
The weakness in this section seems to me to lie in the fact that it is so indefinite. First it provides either that the representatives on this committee may be appointed by the minister or that the minister may authorize certain groups to appoint representatives. Second, the members of this committee may come from two classes of people, either those who market live stock or those who market live stock products. There is no differentiation between them. I do not know how large the committee is going to be, how many are to be appointed by the minister or how many are to be appointed by some group authorized by the minister; I do not know how many delegates on the committee are to be from producers' organizations or processors' organizations. Last year under the minister's department there was a bill which also set up an advisory committee, and it set out the different organizations that would send representatives. speechtext:
Well, we will have the discussion now. I think there is no doubt in the minds of a large proportion of the people of this country who have made a study of the problems of the live stock producer that he is distinctly handicapped in the handling of his products when they are handled in other than a recognized public yard. This part of the bill deals with stockyards. I do not know whether either the agriculture committee or this committee realizes fully the significance of the change that is made in connection with this legislation. When the live stock act was passed originally-I have it here-in so far as it dealt with stockyards the object was gradually to build up public yards where the individual producer would have an opportunity of a square deal in the handling of his products when, in the very nature of things, it was impossible for that producer personally to follow those products to the door of the buyer or to the market. It was assumed that under government supervision the rights of the producer, when his products came to those yards, could be so safeguarded that he would be assured of a square deal.
What the committee is now doing in passing the bill is to a large extent breaking down the control of these public yards that has been built up over the years. Simply because a number of stockyards grew up and, according to the explanatory note six of them did not have live stock exchanges, we are going to throw the thing largely overboard, and the
Live Stock and Poultry

owners of the yards are now to be the people to determine the regulations which will control the handling of producer's stocks sent to those yards for sale.
If there were any need for further illustration of the domination of producer's rights and interests by the most interested party of all, namely the party who buys his goods, certainly we have it in this particular legislation. I have said in the house many times, not because I am opposed to the packing interests, but because I know the packing interests are not the interests of the producers, that the producer has been largely under the domination of the packing interests in this country. I know very well that to-morrow some of the gentlemen in the packing industry will criticize me and say that I am attacking them again. That is not the point. So long as one takes a stand in defence of the rights of the producer he is in conflict with the processor or packer.
In this instance we are indulging in a sort of retrograde movement, and we are doing away with the meagre safeguards which, through the public yards, have been built up over the years. Since the public yards were established and through the evolution of transportation there has grown up this practice of trucking directly to the plants. It is a practice which is very much encouraged by the packers-and it is their right and privilege to do so. I am not questioning their right to do it, so long as there is no law against it. But the wisdom of it, from the point of view of the producer is an entirely different matter. We do know that by the trucking system the producer has been brought more and more under the domination of the buyer of his product. He has no chance at all, except through the ordinary decency dictated by the instincts of good business-and nothing else.
As I was about to say when I was interrupted, and was prevented from doing so, at the present time there are literally, I would venture to say, hundreds of truckers who go out through the country and load up their trucks. In so doing they become the trustees of the farmers' products, just as much as a trust company is trustee of an estate. They carry those hogs or cattle, as the case may be, to the central market, back their truck up to a yard gate, sit on their seats while the truck is unloaded by the buyer and the goods are weighed by the buyer. And, so far as I know, there is little if any supervision in regard to grading-none whatever in regard to cattle, and very little in regard to hogs. The producer of that live stock has no chance 
whatever of a check, and no right to a check on his product. The stockyards did give him a chance, because they were supervised by stock exchanges, and supposed to be checked by officers of the Department of Agriculture.
What we should have had in this live stock measure was some definite stiffening of regulations in connection with the handling of live stock. For instance, there is the matter I have brought up over and over again where a carload-and I am speaking of a railway carload-of hogs may be shipped to a market from some western source, and where the buyer from a large packing plant will come along and refuse to buy at all, unless he can buy all of them. That sort of thing should be stopped. It is known to be going on. Officials of the department know it, and in the last few years there has been plenty of time to work out regulations which would deal with a matter of that kind. I have ideas on it, but it would be futile to express them here. This practice, however, is something which should be stopped. Further, it is entirely wrong to leave to the buyer of the live stock the right of weighing and handling them, and of deciding what should be put on the ticket that is to be handed out.
Without any question we should place in this legislation additional safeguards for the producer-and we are not doing it. On the contrary we are abandoning what little protection he has had, through live stock exchanges controlling these markets.
Let us be perfectly frank about this. The minister will probably know more about the matter than I do, and will correct me if I am wrong; Is not Canada Packers the largest or among the largest of the shareholders of the stockyards in Toronto.

Ofcourse the railway companies are interested in the feeding and watering, and so forth. That is all they are interested in. There is no reflection	upon	the	railroads,	or
upon Sir Edward Beatty or Mr. Hungerford when I say they know nothing about the live stock business. That is not their business. But we are going now to take the great Winnipeg market, the second greatest market in Canada, and turn it over to Sir Edward Beatty and Mr. Hungerford, or to some paid officials under their control.
What about the Edmonton market? I have forgotten the interests which control it. But there was a good public market in Edmonton. Then Canada Packers established a market about a mile and a quarter away, at their plant; and I have all the figures here, but I will not take time to refer to them to-night; I have them here, by the ream, showing the tremendous increase in live stock trucked to the packing plant.

speechtext:
I doubt that very much; I certainly do not believe that, and I have gone very carefully into this matter, many times. On the contrary, I think there is a definite and distinct loss to the producer. But that is not the point. Why are we turning over to the owner of the stockyard the control of the stockyard instead of having what we had before, the live stock exchange? Or
there should be definite control by the government or by the department. Let me come back to this. The idea behind this whole business of public markets is to provide an impartial place where the undefended producer of live stock may send his goods with safety. That was the theory, but we are now abandoning that absolutely. We are turning it right over to the conflicting interests. Again I repeat, because I know I am going to be misunderstood by many, this is a question of simple human nature. One who is the buyer of a thing cannot at the same time serve the seller of the thing. It cannot be done because it is beyond all human nature.

speechtext:
My hon. friend is not
within miles of what I was talking about. The minister knows quite well what I am referring to. What we should have been doing is to put the control more definitely in the department or the government. Not only that, but we should have brought the control of the packer's unloading plant into the same position as that of the public yards. That is what I was hoping would be done. When I read this bill I found that we were making literally no provision for that at all even in the face of the transformation which has taken place in the last few years in this business. I refer to the shipment by truck, which matter was discussed, I think in the agriculture committee and certainly in another committee which sat two, three or four year* ago. This is not a new question; it is something which has been growing up from year to year. We are literally turning the farmer over to the party who is buying his good*. I do not care if he is a saint from heaven, so long as one is more or less afflicted with the frailties of human nature it is impossible for a buyer to give to the seller of goods the treatment to which he is entitled. It is the duty of parliament and the Department of Agriculture above all other departments t* protect the interests of the producers in thi* regard.
